The statement lists a balance of $5,180 and says payment is overdue. Our purchase record shows the invoice was received on 12 August. The underlying invoice is $4,800. It includes a $380 service charge. Quoted reply from Larkspur receiving, 13 August: We dispute the service charge because the service report was signed off on 20 August, after the invoice was received. Per clause 6, a service charge is payable only when its report is approved; if approval occurs after invoice receipt, the charge is due 10 calendar days after approval, separate from the base invoice. The base invoice remains subject to the 45-day term. The vendor also sent a separate $4,800 reminder for another site, but that is not invoice QH-771. Quoted reply from finance lead, 8 September: Do not combine the two dates or add the charge to the base due date. The base amount is due 45 days after 12 August; count the day after receipt as day one. The service charge is due 10 days after 22 August, with the approval date itself excluded. Meeting notes typed from the community services room, 14 June. Present: Greta Kowalski, permit counter clerk; two unnamed residents; note taker. Subject list: garden access permits, a mobility benefit, and follow-up paperwork. Short phrases are retained from the board. A question mark means the group had not confirmed the item at that point; it is not a decision.

Opening: Greta checked the arrivals sheet. One resident had not failed to sign in; their name was on the second line, partly covered by a folded agenda. Do not mark them absent. The sign-in sheet does not establish that they filed any permit application. Greta said the sign-in record and application register are separate.

Garden-access item: Greta described the seasonal plot permit. Applications can ask for one plot or a shared plot. The form in front of the group had “one plot” selected. “Shared?” was written in the margin, but no shared-plot box was checked and nobody asked the clerk to amend the form. The applicant said, “I did not choose shared, not even as a backup.” The clerk repeated that the submitted choice was one plot.

The plot is beside the east path, not the west path. A map with both routes was on the table. The west path is used in the example handout, but that handout is not the submitted map. The resident did not ask to relocate the plot. The east gate is narrow; that may matter for access planning, but the notes do not say anyone requested a gate alteration.

Paperwork: the plot application includes a signed declaration. Greta said it was not unsigned. A copy of the applicant’s address confirmation was also in the file. The soil-test result was not in the file, and the applicant did not claim it was. The desk does not require that result before initial review; it may ask for one later. That possible later request is not evidence that the result was submitted now.

Mobility-benefit item: the person at the table asked whether their bus pass could be considered. Greta clarified that this was a question about eligibility, not a filed claim. The benefit application was not submitted at the meeting. The resident said they had not decided whether to apply and had not filled in the form. The group agreed not to label the inquiry as a request for a payment decision.

The benefit leaflet was left on the table. It lists a monthly transit pass and accessible taxi trips as possible covered services, subject to review. It does not say that both services have been granted to this resident. Greta warned the note taker not to copy the leaflet’s list into the person’s record as an approved benefit. The resident did not ask for accessible taxi trips and did not say they had used them.

Permit fee: the published fee for one plot is £18. The applicant paid £18 at the counter. The receipt was handed over, and the clerk attached it to the application. There is no fee waiver request. “Waiver?” on the agenda was a prompt for discussion of next season’s policy, not a request from the applicant. Nobody said the present fee was unpaid.

Inspection: the applicant did not refuse the inspection. They said they could attend on the date offered, then wrote the date in their diary. The inspector has not yet visited the plot, so the file is not marked inspected. The group discussed what would happen if rain delayed the visit; that was a contingency only, and no postponement was requested.

The second resident asked about a separate permit for a pop-up table at the library. Greta provided a blank form but did not receive a completed form. The resident said, “I have not submitted one, and I am not asking you to open a file today.” The blank form went home with them. This was not the east-path plot application and must not be combined with it.

At the end, Greta reviewed the board: one plot selected; east path; signed declaration; address confirmation; fee paid; soil test not received; inspection pending. She specifically said that “pending” does not mean refused or approved. The group did not vote on the benefit, did not decide the pop-up-table permit, and did not change the plot choice. The note taker read the summary aloud and nobody corrected those points.

Action list: applicant may bring the soil result if requested; clerk will schedule the inspection; resident may decide later whether to submit a mobility-benefit form; second resident may return with the pop-up application. These are future actions, not completed events. No one asked the clerk to close the plot file. The clerk said it remains open for review.

Officer said to keep the permit and benefit folders separate. Rosa agreed and put the blue folder on the left side of the table and the cream folder on the right.

The kiosk was mentioned because it appears in a sample permit guide, but Rosa said she was not asking to run one. Her application asks for a notice board, no sales, no amplified sound. She did ask whether the board could be visible from the footpath, and the officer said the submitted north-gate plan would be reviewed for that. That question does not amend the site requested.

Included with the park application: signed permission from the neighborhood group and a sketch of the proposed board. The permission page is not unsigned. The application fee was not paid at this meeting; Rosa said she would pay after checking whether the neighborhood group could cover it. The fee is still outstanding. The officer did not say that the application was rejected for that reason; it remains under preliminary review.

Rosa did not include a contractor quote. She asked if one was required. The officer said no quote was needed at this stage. A note saying “quote?” is a question, not proof of receipt. The board is not built, and no installation date has been set. Rosa did not ask to start work before the permit decision.

Winter support benefit: Rosa asked whether an older household member might qualify for help with heating costs. She did not submit a benefit application for herself or another person. The meeting did not make an eligibility decision.

The brochure lists heating-bill credit, insulation materials, and emergency fuel delivery as possible forms of assistance, depending on review. These are examples in the brochure, not benefits granted to Rosa. She did not ask for emergency fuel delivery and did not report that her supply had run out. Rosa asked a separate question about whether a transit pass could be covered by a different program. She did not request a transit pass in this meeting and did not fill out that program’s form. The officer said the pass question should go to the mobility desk. Nothing in the meeting notes says that Rosa is currently receiving a transit benefit.

The group reviewed contact preferences. Rosa does not want public notice of her household details; she asked that any benefit form be handled privately if she later applies. This request is about confidentiality, not evidence that a benefit form has already been filed. She did not refuse future contact from the office. She said an email reply is acceptable for permit updates.

At closing, the officer summarized: park application received; north gate requested; neighborhood-group permission and sketch present; fee unpaid; no quote required now; no benefit claim filed. Rosa said the summary was correct and did not ask to withdraw the permit application. She also did not ask the office to treat the benefit inquiry as an application. The note taker marked the park file “open, initial check.”

The officer did not promise approval. No one said a refusal had been issued. Rosa left with the blank benefit form and a copy of the permit receipt page showing the outstanding-fee status. The receipt page is not a payment receipt.

Final note from Rosa, written beside the summary: “I did not ask for a kiosk, and I did not submit benefit paperwork. Please do not combine those things with the board form.” The officer initialed the note and left both folders open for their proper desks.

Account booklet excerpt and service-desk circular — Mateo Lindqvist

Meridian Foods card services, internal customer copy, revised 12 February. This booklet excerpt explains dates for purchase disputes and does not decide whether a particular merchant was at fault. Mateo Lindqvist attached it to his inquiry about a recurring grocery delivery plan. His statement uses the merchant name Meridian Foods. This material is for cardholders and service staff; the examples are invented illustrations from the booklet and are not Mateo’s transactions.

Section 1. When a clock begins. For a posted purchase, the posting date is day zero when the rule expressly says “after posting.” Count calendar days, not weekdays, unless the relevant row specifically says business days. The following calendar date is day one. A date shown as “received” in the portal is the filing date. A phone call, a draft, a saved document, or a message to the merchant does not substitute for receipt. If the last permitted date is a weekend or holiday, the deadline remains that date under the standard rule; there is no automatic next-business-day extension. If an individual case receives a written extension, use the extension’s stated new date instead.

Section 2. Service not provided. A cardholder may submit a service-not-provided dispute after first asking the merchant to perform or refund. The request must arrive within 45 calendar days after the promised service date. The promised service date is day zero for this particular rule, rather than the purchase posting date. If the merchant gives a new specific service date in writing, use the newest agreed date. A vague statement such as “soon” does not reset the date. If the service is delivered in parts, the date for the missing part is the date stated for that part, if stated. Staff must not assume that the date of a later phone conversation changes the original promised date.

Section 3. Duplicate processing. If the same purchase appears twice, the standard window is 20 calendar days after the second posting. Count the second posting as day zero. Do not use the first posting merely because it appears earlier on the statement. This section covers a true duplicate charge, not two separate purchases for the same amount. If the cardholder reports two payments for two different orders, staff should record both dates and ask which transaction is being disputed. Amount similarity alone does not establish duplication.

Section 4. Price or amount mismatch. A cardholder reporting that the settled amount differs from the agreed amount must file within 30 calendar days of posting. If the receipt shows a currency conversion, compare the settled local-currency figure shown on the statement with the signed total after any disclosed conversion. Do not add a tip unless the receipt shows one. This paragraph does not say that all unfamiliar currency movements are errors. Staff should preserve the receipt, the settlement entry, and any merchant explanation.

Section 5. Network service interruption. When the bank’s own payment network prevented submission, a cardholder may have a 3-business-day extension, but only if the network incident number is included and the interruption overlapped the final three calendar days of the ordinary filing period. Business days mean Monday through Friday and exclude the two holidays printed in the annual calendar. A routine browser error, forgotten password, merchant website outage, or device problem is not a bank network interruption. The service desk cannot create an extension verbally. A manager must issue a written extension notice.

Section 6. Examples. Example A: purchase posts June 2; a 30-calendar-day rule has June 2 as day zero and July 2 as day 30. Example B: promised delivery is August 10; under the service-not-provided rule, August 10 is day zero and the 45th day is September 24. Example C: two identical-looking charges post October 1 and October 5; for a duplicate claim, October 5 is day zero and October 25 is day 20. Example D: last eligible filing date is Sunday; absent a written exception, Sunday remains the final date. These examples use ordinary dates and are not adjusted for local time differences.

Mateo’s inquiry cover sheet is attached: “Please identify the correct rule for each concern. I am not asking the desk to choose whether I win. I want to know whether each date is in time.” His three line items follow. First, a prepared-food subscription order posted 8 March. The receipt says delivery was promised for 15 March, but no box arrived. His first portal submission for this concern is recorded 28 April. He contacted Meridian Foods on 20 March, and the company wrote back on 23 March, “We are checking.” There is no later promised date in that exchange. Second, one grocery order for $63.20 was posted 6 April and another, separate order for $63.20 was posted 9 April. The receipts have different basket numbers and different item lists. Mateo’s portal submission for the first order is recorded 27 April. He says the two amounts looking alike made him worry about a duplicate, but he purchased both orders. Third, a pantry delivery posted 1 May for $88. The signed order says $80 before delivery and handling, and the final statement amount is $88. The receipt lists an $8 delivery fee agreed at checkout. He submitted a question on 1 June, but this item is not described as a dispute in the portal.

Service-desk scratchpad: a representative wrote that Mateo had “45 days from posting” for the missing box. A supervisor drew a line through this note and pointed to Section 2: service-not-provided is timed from the promised service date. A separate desk comment says, “There are forty-five days between the dates, so likely fine.” The booklet says day zero counts as the stated date, and gives an example to show that the last day is the forty-fifth following calendar date, not forty-five elapsed full-day intervals. No written exception is recorded on Mateo’s account. The bank network was operating normally; there is no incident number. The representative did not issue an extension.

A second scratchpad note says not to mark the two $63.20 entries as a duplicate merely because their amounts match. Section 3 requires a claim about the same purchase being processed twice. Mateo’s cover sheet instead confirms separate basket numbers and two different item lists. Nevertheless, if applying that section’s timing only for the purpose of checking the duplicate-rule date, the second posting is the starting date. The file shows his 27 April portal receipt. The handbook’s staff note says the substantive fit of a rule and the deadline calculation are separate questions: a timely date does not transform two distinct purchases into a duplicate.

Appendix: date-counting worksheet. March has 31 days. Starting after March 15, March 16 is day 1; March 31 is day 16; April 1 is day 17; April 29 is day 45. The 28 April portal receipt would therefore fall before the last day under Section 2, if the section’s stated date is the right one. For the duplicate example, starting after April 9, April 10 is day 1 and April 29 is day 20. The 27 April receipt falls before that final day. For the amount mismatch item, May 1 is day zero; May 31 is day 30. The June 1 inquiry is later than the ordinary final date, but the $8 fee was disclosed and agreed, so the booklet does not say this is an amount mismatch. No one should infer a right to dispute from a late inquiry simply because the amount is easy to calculate.

Staff reminder: do not count from a phone call if the rule names posting or promised service date. Do not treat a later merchant investigation message as a new promise unless it gives a specific new performance date accepted by the cardholder. Do not silently convert calendar days to business days. If a written extension exists, retain the notice and recompute against its stated date. There is no such notice in Mateo’s material. His account has no standing special terms that replace this excerpt.

Mateo wrote at the bottom: “The support person said perhaps they count from when I called merchant. This booklet seems to say not like that. Also 45 days might sound many, but I want actual date. I do not say all three are same problem. The first is absent delivery, second is two different purchases, third I agreed the fee. Please answer by date, not by saying general policy.”

This worksheet was prepared for a Tidewater Outfitters card claim by Rosa Moreau. Rosa says she is writing in simple English because she wants the dates checked carefully. Her dispute concerns a card charge for a waterproof lantern. The bank statement identifies the merchant as Tidewater Outfitters and shows $146 posted 10 September. A separate outdoor-store purchase for $146 posted 12 September belongs to her cousin and is not part of this claim. Rosa has attached the order confirmation, merchant messages, a calendar page, and the card issuer’s time-limit note.

Order confirmation, 29 August: “Lantern order accepted. Estimated delivery September 5. This date is the service promise for purposes of our late delivery review unless both parties agree in writing to a replacement date.” The same page says packing normally takes two days, delivery estimates are not guarantees for weather events, and refund requests must be received within 12 calendar days after the applicable promise date. The promise date is day zero. The page does not say business days. A side banner says delivery estimates are “often earlier than actual arrival.” Rosa says she did not rely on the banner as a promise date.

Merchant message, 3 September: “We have a warehouse delay. We expect your parcel around September 9.” Rosa replied, “Can we make Sept 9 the new agreed delivery date?” The merchant responded, “This is only an estimate, not a replacement promise. The original date remains on the order; sorry for confusion.” Rosa wrote in her calendar, “Sept 9 forecast only.” The order page did not change. No other written exchange agrees to a new promise date.

Carrier tracking shows label made September 2, carrier pickup September 6, regional depot September 8, delivered to parcel room September 11 at 18:40. Rosa collected it September 12. The packaging was intact and the lantern worked. Her dispute is not for nondelivery, damage, or price difference. She says it arrived too late to take on a planned camping weekend, which began September 7. A weather advisory for the region was issued September 4, but the order page does not say that weather automatically shifts the deadline. Rosa does not ask the bank to decide whether the weather should excuse the seller.

Rosa contacted the merchant September 12 at 09:05. Her message says, “I received package yesterday in building room. I want late-delivery refund because not here before weekend.” The merchant replied September 13: “Our system shows delivery estimate September 9 and arrival September 11. We can offer store credit.” Rosa declined the credit on September 14. The conversation does not state that the original promise was formally changed. A customer-service agent wrote on a separate internal note, “Customer agreed to wait until Sept 9,” but Rosa says she did not. The only written exchange shows her asking whether September 9 could be made a new date and the merchant explicitly saying it was only an estimate.

Bank note copied from the account portal: “For a late-service delivery request, submit within 12 calendar days after the applicable promise date. The promise date is day zero; the following date is day one. Calendar days include Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. If merchant and customer agree in writing to a new specific promise date, that replacement date becomes day zero. A forecast, tracking estimate, or one-sided internal note does not replace the written order promise. Submission is received only when the portal displays a receipt number. Merchant contact and refusal of store credit do not pause or restart the clock.”

Rosa’s portal log has several entries. Draft opened September 15 at 20:17. Receipt number generated September 17 at 08:22. A failed upload on September 16 at 21:50 has no receipt number. She wrote to herself, “I think I finish on 16 but portal still loading.” The bank’s log says the successful receipt was on September 17. The portal help page says saving a draft preserves text but does not submit a dispute. There is no extension note, no network incident number, and no manager letter extending the deadline.

A neighbor’s order is shown in an attached email by mistake: lantern ordered August 27, expected delivery September 4, actually delivered September 6, dispute submitted September 16. Rosa crossed it out and wrote, “not my card transaction.” Another amount in the statement is $14.60 for a camping fuel canister. A handwritten line reads “$146 lantern, not $14.60 fuel.” The fuel purchase is dated September 7 and is unrelated. These entries were included because the portal asked for nearby transactions, not because Rosa disputes them.

A handwritten computation at the bottom reads: “If Sept 5 is day 0: Sept 6=1, Sept 12=7, Sept 17=12.” She then crosses out the last part and writes, “Wait: counting carefully, Sept 6=1; Sept 12=7; Sept 17=12 yes.” The bank worksheet confirms the calculation: September 5 day zero; September 6 day one; September 17 day twelve. The last permitted date is September 17, inclusive, because the rule says “within 12 days” and specifically defines the twelfth following calendar date as the final date. Rosa’s portal receipt at 08:22 on September 17 is therefore on the last permitted day, if September 5 remains the applicable promise date.

A second possible calculation appears in a customer-service reply: “If the date were September 9, then September 10 is day one and September 21 is day twelve.” This is arithmetically consistent but depends on a replacement date being agreed in writing. The record does not show that agreement. The message calls September 9 an estimate and retains the original date. A staff member’s internal note cannot change what the customer and merchant agreed under the rule. The carrier’s September 11 delivery date is also not an agreed new promise date.

Rosa says she is not claiming the delivery took twelve days after the initial date; she is asking whether the filing was inside the rule’s exact window. She understands actual delivery, opening a draft, and contacting the merchant may feel relevant but the bank note lists the controlling dates. Dispute policy page and case appendix — Beatriz Tanaka

Meridian Foods cardholder operations guide, revision 4, copied with Beatriz Tanaka’s statement query. This guide gives time limits for three different kinds of purchase concerns. It is not an assessment of whether the merchant acted properly. Each clock uses the date named in its own section. Staff should not use one section’s start date for another type of concern simply because all entries appear on the same card statement. All dates are local dates as displayed in the portal.

Rule A, unauthorized recurring charge: request must be received within 25 calendar days after the charge posts. Posting date is day zero. The service cancellation date is not the start date for this rule. If a charge is authorized but disputed because the service continued after a cancellation request, use Rule B instead. A charge description that says “subscription” does not by itself establish that the charge was unauthorized.

Rule B, cancellation not honored: when the merchant receives a cancellation request and subsequently posts another recurring charge, the cardholder must file within 18 calendar days after that later charge posts. The later charge is day zero. The initial cancellation request does not start the bank filing window. A merchant email confirming a cancellation may establish what service was requested to stop, but does not change the posting date from which the bank filing window is measured. A later reversal or credit does not erase the original posting date for the purpose of deciding whether an initial dispute was timely.

Rule C, merchandise not received: file within 35 calendar days after the last promised delivery date. The stated promise date is day zero unless the customer and merchant agree in writing to a specific replacement date. A carrier forecast is not such an agreement. A later delivery does not reset the period. If the order lists separate promised dates for separate items, apply the date for the item claimed missing. Day counting includes weekends and holidays. The portal receipt date decides when a filing was received; a customer’s call or saved draft does not count.

The guide gives these examples. If a charge posts on January 1 under Rule A, January 26 is day 25. If a later recurring charge posts on February 4 under Rule B, February 22 is day 18. If a package is promised for March 10 under Rule C, April 14 is day 35. The specific sections take priority over the general account leaflet, which says disputes should be submitted promptly but gives no different numerical period. No automatic extension applies for a weekend. A written extension notice must state the new final date.

Beatriz’s first statement line is a Meridian Foods monthly pantry membership charge of $29, posted November 2. She says she had signed up for the membership and used it for the prior month. She sent a cancellation request October 20, and Meridian Foods replied October 21, “Membership will stop before next renewal; no further monthly amount expected.” A further $29 charge posted November 2. Beatriz submitted a portal dispute November 21, receipt number visible. She asks whether this is inside the appropriate filing period. The account shows no reversal, no extension notice, and no later replacement charge.

Her second line is a different recurring service: an optional spice-box plan for $17, posted November 3. Beatriz says she did not recognize the plan and never signed up. The merchant records show that she enrolled online on September 30, but she disputes that the enrollment record is hers. The portal request for this line was received November 28. The file includes this contested enrollment detail only to distinguish the type of claim; the time calculation in Rule A uses the posting date. A one-line bank annotation says, “November charge, so count from cancellation?” The section text says unauthorized recurring charges are counted from posting, while cancellation-not-honored claims use the later recurring charge under Rule B.

Her third line is a pair of ceramic storage jars ordered October 1. The confirmation promised delivery October 10. On October 8, the merchant wrote, “A delay is possible; tracking currently estimates October 13.” Beatriz replied, “Please let me know,” and the merchant answered, “We cannot change your original promise date.” The jars did not arrive by October 10, but the carrier delivered October 15. Beatriz submitted a merchandise-not-received inquiry on November 14, with portal receipt number. She says the carrier’s October 13 forecast was not accepted as a new promise date. No separate item date or written extension appears.

A fourth line is unrelated: an $82 grocery order posted November 6, correctly delivered November 7. Beatriz’s spouse ordered it on the shared card with permission. She marked it “not disputed.” A fifth line is a $17 cafe payment posted November 9; it is not a recurring plan. These entries are on the same statement because the portal exported the whole month. Neither is part of her request. The statement also includes a $34 refund posted November 16 for a different returned item; it does not refer to the membership or spice plan.

Portal activity details: membership claim draft began November 19 and received November 21. Spice-box claim draft began November 26 and received November 28. Jar claim draft began November 12 and received November 14. The receipt time is logged in local time, but each date falls on an ordinary calendar day with no date boundary issue. The guide says calendar counting, not business-day counting. There is no bank outage record, and all submissions have receipt numbers.

Case analyst’s date worksheet: Rule B for the membership: November 2 is day zero, November 3 day one; November 20 day 18. Receipt November 21 is day 19 and outside. The cancellation email October 21 is not the filing clock start. Rule A for the spice-box line: November 3 is day zero, November 4 day one; November 28 is day 25. Receipt November 28 is day 25 and within the deadline. Rule C for jars: October 10 is day zero, October 11 day one; November 14 is day 35. Receipt November 14 is day 35 and within. The guide treats the last stated day as eligible.

There is a handwritten note from a first-line representative: “The cancelled plan was stopped Oct 20, therefore 18 days runs from then to Nov 7; maybe too late.” The policy says otherwise: Rule B’s clock starts from the later charge posting, not the cancellation request. A different representative wrote, “The box forecast says Oct 13 so use that date.” This also conflicts with Rule C: the merchant said it was not changing the promise, and a tracking forecast is not an agreement. Beatriz’s own notes quote the written exchange rather than asking the bank to infer consent from silence.

Appendix on day counting: To count a specified number after a date, exclude the named date as day zero and count each following calendar date. For November 2 plus 18 days: Nov 3 is 1, Nov 10 is 8, Nov 20 is 18. For November 3 plus 25: Nov 4 is 1, Nov 28 is 25. For October 10 plus 35: Oct 11 is 1, Oct 31 is 21, Nov 14 is 35. These counts are based on the calendar, not the number of work shifts or elapsed hours. No holiday adjustment is permitted by this guide.

I cancelled one plan and still got next charge; the other I say was not my enrollment; jars came after promise but later tracking was not agreed date. I know call person used same phrase ‘subscription dispute’ for first two, but rule page gives different start and limit. The counter clerk wrote that it was “not fair to make her chase us for arithmetic,” but did not authorize a payment or change the register.

The same queue includes a receipt for 36 on Sella’s reproduction line, of which 24 is paid; the remainder is 12. It is not a 36-dollar balance. Her evening inspection total is 160 and half, 80, has been recorded as paid, leaving 80. The curb access line is 275 assessed less 200 paid, leaving 75. 1. Recalculate balances using assessed total minus payment; do not use assessed totals as unpaid balances.
2. For current benefit totals by recipient, add only the entries in the approved current amount column.
3. Keep permit balances and benefits on their separate sides of the report.
4. Do not treat requested amounts, earlier-period amounts, sample cases, suggested adjustments, or unapproved notes as awarded money.
5. If an applicant’s form includes a correct arithmetic note, verify it against the line items rather than accepting or rejecting it based on tone.

The checklist was drafted after a tense meeting. One participant yelled that “all the numbers are lies,” while another said the queue was “perfectly clear.” Neither statement changes any recorded amount. A page in the packet repeats the number 190 as a sample permit balance for an unrelated training exercise. It happens also to be the correct sum of Harbor’s two open permit balances, but the sample is not evidence about Harbor; the line-item differences in Harbor’s ledger are the evidence. Another appendix repeats 470 as a generic example benefit award. It lists 3, 6, and 12 in a diagnostic column for rows with zero, partial, and full payment records; these are counts grouped by status and are not applicant totals. A staff member copied “six benefits, 1,695” into a note by summing several different amounts, including requests and prior-period values. That number is not a valid total of current approved benefits. The approved-current register rows themselves are the controlling evidence.

A later validation read the figures aloud: Dmitri current approved 450 plus 120 equals 570; Harbor current approved 360 plus 110 equals 470; Sella current approved 325 plus 100 equals 425? The reviewer immediately crossed out 425 and corrected the sum to 425 only after checking: 325 + 100 is 425. The written correction is retained to show the check, not to suggest another value. Sella’s separate call note saying 490 was based on including the 65 earlier-period amount. The exact current total remains the sum of the two approved current entries.

APPENDIX B — PORTAL DEFINITIONS
“Assessed total” is the full charge entered for a permit line. “Payment recorded” is the amount received and matched. “Balance” is the unpaid difference for that line. “Current approved amount” is the awarded amount for the present benefit period. “Earlier-period amount” is a prior decision and is not part of a current award total. “Requested amount” is the applicant’s request before determination. A field may contain a numerically plausible figure and still be the wrong field for the question being asked.

The portal help page also describes a possible refund pathway, an optional 25-dollar new permit application fee, a 10-dollar document replacement fee, and a sample benefit payment of 500. None of those general examples is a transaction in the three cases above. The Harbor form explicitly selects correction of a public access record and says “Refund requested: No.” The sentence “I am not asking you to refund a fee” is consistent with that field. The update is angry, but anger does not turn its category into a refund or alter the numerical calculations.

CLOSING COMMENT FROM OREN

They are asking us to subtract the paid amount from the assessed total and to add the right approved benefit rows. If the manager’s next briefing repeats the 560 figure for Harbor, someone will again have to explain why a prior-period 90 was quietly promoted to a current award. The ledger is already enough of a mess without that.

ATTACHED POLICY EXTRACT — TRANSITION PAYMENT, VERSION EFFECTIVE 1 JULY 2026

1. Scope and defined dates

1.1 “Last scheduled workday” means the final day on which the employee was scheduled to perform work in the relevant role. It does not mean the day the employee first discussed leaving, the date a manager entered a calendar note, or the date payroll completed its calculations.

1.2 “Submission date” means the local calendar date and time recorded on the automatically generated People Operations receipt. An employee’s draft, an email asking about a form, a manager’s acknowledgment, and a calendar entry are not submissions.

1.3 “Calendar day” means every consecutive day, including weekends and holidays. A period measured in calendar days begins on the day after the triggering event. The triggering date is day zero. A request received by 23:59 local time on the final counted day is timely. The rule does not convert calendar days to business days.

1.4 “Transition payment” is a one-time payment considered after an employee’s final scheduled workday. This extract does not determine the amount of any payment and does not promise payment merely because a form is timely.

2. Filing window

2.1 An employee is eligible for an ordinary review of a transition-payment request if the employee submits the standard form no later than fourteen calendar days after the last scheduled workday.

2.2 A request submitted after that fourteen-day period is not eligible for ordinary review. It is not the case that a request submitted after the period remains eligible merely because the employee previously told a manager that a form might be filed. A conversation, reminder, draft, or unsubmitted attachment does not stop or restart the clock.

2.3 The policy does not say that an employee is ineligible when a timely receipt exists. Conversely, the absence of a timely receipt cannot be cured by a later statement that the employee intended to file before the deadline.

2.4 The last scheduled workday is day zero, not day one. For example, if the last scheduled workday is 3 May, 4 May is day one and 17 May is day fourteen. The deadline is the end of 17 May. A submission on 18 May is late.

3. Narrow extension

3.1 The only extension in this extract applies when the People Operations form service is unavailable continuously for at least six hours during the final calendar day of the filing window. The employee must submit the form by 23:59 on the first calendar day after service is restored and attach the automatically generated outage reference.

3.2 A slow page, an employee’s inability to locate a link, a payroll question, a manager’s absence, or an outage lasting less than six continuous hours does not qualify. It is not enough that the employee cannot rule out the possibility of a brief interruption; the system log must show the qualifying outage and the case file must contain the reference.

3.3 The extension does not apply to a form filed after its extended deadline. It does not apply if the service was functioning during the final filing day, even if the employee found the form confusing or chose to wait for another document.

4. Review and status

4.1 A portal status of “received,” “pending,” or “under review” confirms receipt or processing only. No such status by itself means that the request is approved or rejected.

4.2 A manager’s statement that the employee is “not denied” is not an approval. A manager cannot waive the filing period through email. People Operations applies this extract to the receipt, work schedule, and service log.

4.3 If evidence conflicts, use the automatic receipt for submission time, the finalized schedule for the last scheduled workday, and the system availability log for any claimed outage. Do not substitute a person’s estimate for a timestamp.

PEOPLE OPERATIONS REVIEW CHECKLIST — GENERAL USE

This checklist is attached to the file because reviewers use the same packet to assess leave events, payment requests, and annual attestations. It is not a substitute for the controlling clause or timestamp. Each item is written as a question to be answered from records, not from an employee’s prediction about what may happen.

A. Identify the applicable version

A1. Locate the signed amendment register entry with an effective date covering the event. Do not apply a circulated proposal unless the register says it was executed and incorporated.

A2. If two passages appear inconsistent, check for a later signed clarification. A later clarification may explain the earlier language without changing its effective date. Do not treat the mere presence of an older passage in an archived document as proof that it remains controlling.

A3. Record the triggering event from the designated record. For filing periods, use the finalized schedule. For form filing, use the automatic receipt. For service outages, use the service log and required reference.

A4. Count according to the policy’s own definition. Do not silently substitute business days for calendar days, count the triggering day when it is expressly excluded, or add time for a weekend unless the rule says to do so.

B. Interpret statements about negation carefully

B1. “I am not saying that I will not file” expresses that the employee has not ruled out filing. It does not establish that a form was filed.

B2. “The request is not denied” means no denial has been stated. It does not mean approved, eligible, timely, or paid.

B3. “It is not the case that the filing is not timely” is a double-negative construction. Resolve it by determining whether the actual receipt is within the applicable window; do not assign meaning by counting the word “not.”

B4. A future conditional, such as “if the form is late, I will appeal,” is not evidence that the form is currently late or that an appeal has been filed.

B5. A person may accurately say, “I am not claiming the form was received on my last shift,” while still having filed inside the actual deadline. Distinguish the first day of the window from the last day of the window.

C. Do not infer events from administrative shorthand

C1. “Pending” is a workflow state. “Not denied” is an absence of an adverse decision. Neither one establishes approval.

C2. “Possible final shift,” “wrap-up,” and “payroll check” are not schedule changes unless the finalized schedule is amended.

C3. An employee’s intent to submit, a manager’s awareness, or a draft saved on a device is not the receipt timestamp defined in the policy.

C4. An informal message saying “the portal was down” is not a qualifying outage unless the system log and required reference meet section 3.

D. Keep distinct decisions distinct

D1. A determination that a form is timely is not itself a determination of payment amount.

D2. A determination that a person remains eligible for review does not guarantee that every substantive payment condition is met.

D3. A determination that a person is not eligible under the filing window should identify the date calculation and any claimed exception that was checked.

D4. Where the question asks whether the evidence supports a specified conclusion, answer from the evidence in the packet. Do not supply a broader conclusion than the records permit.

E. Common calendar examples

E1. Last scheduled workday 10 June; the next day is day one. Day fourteen is 24 June. A receipt on 24 June at 23:59 is timely; a receipt on 25 June is not.

E2. Last scheduled workday 28 February in a non-leap year; 1 March is day one. The reviewer must count fourteen consecutive calendar dates, including weekends. Do not assume that a month boundary resets the clock.

E3. If an employee submits on day eleven, the fact that submission was “after the last shift” is immaterial to timeliness. The deadline is not the same day as the triggering event.

E4. If an employee submits on day fifteen, a manager’s earlier reassurance that the request has “not been denied” does not make the submission timely. Check the receipt, not the reassurance.

F. Recordkeeping

F1. Preserve the original schedule, signed amendments, receipt, and service log in the case file. A summary should not replace source records when a disputed date is at issue.

F2. If the reviewer notices that a date in an email differs from a timestamp, note the discrepancy and use the designated timestamp. Do not average dates or choose whichever is more favorable without a rule.

F3. If the packet contains a draft amendment, identify its status. Do not quote it as if it were effective merely because it appears in the same attachment set.

F4. Keep a short explanation of the arithmetic. For example: “1 September is day zero; 2–15 September are days 1–14; receipt on 12 September is day 11.”

F5. A statement that nobody has said “no” does not establish that the answer is “yes.” A statement that a person has not said “never” does not establish that the person has already acted.

POLICY INTERPRETATION MEMO: NEGATIVE FORMS AND DEADLINE QUESTIONS

Purpose
This memo helps reviewers interpret ordinary-language statements that include one or more negations. It is not a rule changing any filing deadline. The controlling date remains the date in the applicable policy and the evidence remains the designated record.

Examples relevant to the attached records

• “I am not saying I will never file” does not equal “I filed.” The speaker is declining to rule out a future action.
• “I have not failed to file on time” can mean that the speaker has not missed the deadline, but it must be checked against the dates. If the deadline has not passed, the statement does not establish completion.
• “It is not the case that the request is not timely” is equivalent, in ordinary formal logic, to saying that the request is timely. In case handling, verify that the premise corresponds to a real receipt and the applicable count.
• “Not denied” is not equivalent to “approved.” It states only that a denial has not occurred or has not been communicated.
• “No evidence that it was not submitted” is not the same as affirmative evidence that it was submitted. Locate the receipt.
• “Not no longer eligible” can be syntactically confusing. Avoid deciding from the phrase alone; restate the underlying proposition in plain language and compare the dates.

A reviewer should not assume that a person’s use of a double negative is deliberate legal drafting. Record the underlying event, then state the result without relying on wordplay. The language in messages is evidence of what the writer said, not a substitute for the official timestamp.

Sample decision language:
“The receipt shows submission on 12 September. The last scheduled workday was 1 September, which is day zero. The fourteen calendar days run from 2 through 15 September, inclusive. The receipt is therefore within the ordinary filing period. The record supports eligibility for ordinary review on timeliness, but does not itself establish final approval or payment.”

Do not write:
“She said she was not not late, therefore she is approved.”
That sentence confuses a statement about timing with the distinct question of substantive approval.

Do not write:
“The manager did not deny the claim, so the claim is accepted.”
That sentence turns absence of a denial into affirmative approval, contrary to the status rule.

Do not write:
“She did not file on her last shift, so the request is late.”
That sentence ignores the full fourteen-day period and fails to count from the day after the trigger.

Related worked examples for reviewers

Example 1: A worker’s last scheduled day is 4 October. The receipt is dated 19 October. 5 October is day one; 18 October is day fourteen. The receipt on 19 October is day fifteen and is outside the ordinary window. A statement that the employee “did not miss the deadline” is contradicted by the records. If no qualifying extension applies, the request is not eligible for ordinary review under this filing rule.

Example 2: A worker’s last scheduled day is 4 October. The receipt is dated 17 October. 5 October is day one; 17 October is day thirteen. The request is inside the ordinary window. The fact that the worker did not file on 4 October does not make it late. A message saying “I am not not within the period” is clumsy but consistent with the date calculation.

Example 3: A worker’s last scheduled day is 4 October, and no receipt exists by 19 October. A saved draft and a manager’s comment that the worker is “not denied” do not prove filing. The reviewer cannot label the request timely without the receipt. If the question is whether evidence supports a timely filing, the answer is not supported by these records.

Example 4: A worker’s last scheduled day is 4 October; the filing deadline is 18 October. The service log records an outage from 18 October 20:00 to 19 October 02:30, six and one-half continuous hours, and supplies the required reference. A form received by 23:59 on 20 October meets the stated extension rule, assuming all listed evidence is present. An outage lasting only from 20:00 to 23:30 would be three and one-half hours and would not qualify.

These examples deliberately use dates different from Nadia’s file. They explain how to apply the counting method, not what happened in the attached case. A reviewer must not copy an example’s outcome without checking the actual schedule and receipt.

TERMS-OF-SERVICE EXCERPT, version 4.2, signed by Granite Dental and Copperleaf Logistics

1. Parties and covered work
Granite Dental (“Customer”) appoints Copperleaf Logistics (“Provider”) to transport sealed dental supply cases between the Customer’s listed clinics and the Provider’s regional holding facility. The parties agree that the schedule and this excerpt form one contract. A clinic employee is not a separate contracting party merely because that employee signs a delivery receipt. The parties’ names in an email header do not alter which party made a request; the body of a message and its sender determine that. “Service day” means a Monday through Friday on which the Provider’s receiving office is open, excluding the closure dates listed in the schedule. A day stated as a calendar day includes weekends and holidays. If a rule says “within N days after receipt,” the receipt date is day zero, and the next calendar day is day one, unless the rule expressly says business days.

2. Monthly charges and credits
The base monthly route fee is $4,800. The two scheduled clinic handling fees are $275 and $325 per month. A separate $150 refrigeration-monitoring charge applies only during a month in which the Customer has requested temperature-controlled carriage in writing. The current file contains no such request for July. A charge appearing on an invoice is not, by itself, proof that the service was requested or performed.

If a route is missed, the Customer may claim a service credit of $180 for that route, but only where the Provider’s dispatch record confirms that the route was not completed. A delayed route is not a missed route if the sealed case was delivered on the same calendar date. A route that is merely described as “not not completed” in an informal note must be read in context: the phrase is a double negative, not a reliable dispatch outcome by itself. The signed dispatch record controls. No party may count the same route twice, whether under a clinic complaint and a billing ticket or under two differently named route codes.

For the monthly adjustment, first add the base route fee and the applicable handling fees; then subtract confirmed service credits. Do not add a fee that the schedule says is inapplicable. An adjustment is approved if the resulting undisputed service charge is no more than $5,300. A bill above $5,300 is not automatically a breach if it includes a clearly separately itemized, disputed charge; it must still be reviewed, and the disputed item is not treated as an approved service charge. The threshold is a comparison of the computed charge with $5,300, not of the invoice’s gross face value.

3. Notice of a billing dispute
A billing dispute must be delivered to the Provider’s contract-notice inbox within 30 calendar days after the Customer receives the invoice. The inbox receipt log, not the date typed in the Customer’s letter, determines delivery. A message sent to a clinic driver, copied to the account manager, or saved as a draft is not delivery to the contract-notice inbox. The notice must identify the invoice and the amount disputed. It need not use the word “dispute” if its substance clearly says the amount is challenged. A notice received on day 30 is timely; a notice received after day 30 is not.

The Customer does not lose the right to dispute an item merely because it did not fail to object earlier: this is intentionally a double-negative formulation used in the negotiated text. Read the following sentence together with it: the right is preserved only if notice is actually delivered within the 30-day period and includes the invoice number and disputed amount. Silence before the deadline is not a delivered notice. An assertion that the Customer “didn’t not object” does not substitute for a logged notice.

4. Route-performance claims
A route-performance claim is separate from a billing dispute. The Customer may claim a credit for a missed route if it files within 10 calendar days after the route date and supplies the route identifier. A route claim received on day 10 is timely. The Provider may reject the claim if the signed record shows delivery on that date, even if the delivery was late in the day. In a conflict between a draft dispatch screen and a signed final record, the signed final record controls. A route shown as “not failed” means it passed; it does not mean it failed. A witness’s statement that it “wasn’t not delivered” is inconclusive until checked against the signed record.

5. Credits, offsets, and payment direction
Credits approved under section 2 reduce the amount the Customer owes the Provider. They do not create a debt owed by the Customer to the Provider. If the Provider has collected an excess amount after an approved credit, the Provider must return that excess to the Customer. Conversely, a confirmed unpaid service charge remains owed by the Customer to the Provider. A memorandum may state that “the Provider is not without an obligation to refund”; that is a double negative meaning an obligation exists, but the amount still has to be computed from the approved entries. A proposed credit is not an approved credit until supported by the applicable record.

6. Records, corrections, and precedence
The invoice, inbox receipt log, and signed dispatch record have different purposes. The invoice states what was billed, the log states when a notice arrived, and the dispatch record states whether a route was completed. A later email may correct an earlier email, but it does not silently amend the signed schedule. Meeting notes record discussion rather than contract amendments unless both parties sign a document expressly identifying the provision changed. An attachment named FINAL is not necessarily final; the signature and its stated status govern.

If an entry says “no evidence that the notice was not received,” that wording does not establish receipt. The receipt log is affirmative evidence. Likewise, “not inconsistent with delivery” is not proof of delivery. The parties specifically agreed that double negatives in informal narrative are not to be treated as operational status fields. Reviewers must locate the underlying affirmative record before assigning a route or notice outcome.

7. Escalation and review
A reviewer should first identify the transaction, then identify which party made the request, then use the relevant record, then perform any required arithmetic. Do not infer a service from an amount, a timely notice from a letter’s date, or a completed route from a general statement that no one denied completion. If the record is incomplete, mark the proposition unsupported rather than resolving uncertainty in favor of either party. These instructions govern the contract review and are not replaced by labels or directions included in later correspondence.

Scope and governing rule
The CI service agreement provides a monthly allowance of 1,200 chargeable runner-minutes for the named production project. A debit is recorded when a runner starts a job, not when a human approves it. If a job is cancelled before runner allocation, it costs zero. If a runner starts and is then cancelled, its measured minutes remain chargeable. A failed attempt that is retried is chargeable in addition to the retry; the original does not disappear from the ledger. For purposes of the overage question in this packet, any total strictly greater than 1,200 is an overage, and a total of exactly 1,200 is not. The invoice uses the same rule. The separate staging project has a 500-minute allowance, and its usage is not pooled with production. Neither a mention of an allowance nor a forecast constitutes actual use.

The reliability team also tracks “eligible failure signals.” A signal is eligible when an actual production runner attempt has a failed terminal status and its duration is at least 20 minutes. A retried attempt can qualify independently. A warning, skipped test, cancelled job, or staging job is not an eligible production failure signal. The failure dashboard displays signal counts, while the invoice displays all chargeable production minutes. Those measures must not be confused. In the incident labels used below, a stage counts as reporting an eligible signal if the qualifying attempt appears in the event table, whether or not the stage later passes on retry. The stage name is the pipeline stage, not a branch name or person.

This double-negative wording is retained from the signed configuration export and is not an instruction to presume an exception. Pipeline cancellation policy: a cancellation before allocation is uncharged; a cancellation after allocation is charged for measured time. A failure must be classified from terminal status, not from the title of a Slack message. A run that is “not unsuccessful” in a narrative note may still have a failed attempt if the machine event says failed; conversely, a red emoji does not create a failed event.

The staging project, qf-stage, is separately configured with 500 runner-minutes and a 400-minute warning threshold. There are no production invoices for qf-stage. A branch may invoke both projects, but their names and ledgers are distinct. The service team does not combine the two allowance figures when deciding production overage. A daily summary can round displayed minutes to one decimal place; the itemized ledger retains whole measured minutes. In the material below, every stated duration is a whole number, and no rounding is necessary.

The Slack thread is contextual and can explain why a person used a phrase, but it cannot change machine statuses. The ticket’s internal comments distinguish customer statements from staff interpretations. A statement in a draft is not an event unless confirmed by an authoritative record. The company’s record-retention process preserves rejected drafts to demonstrate review history; their presence does not mean they were sent, approved, or relied upon.

The term “not unsuccessful” in one note is not a formal CI state. The formal states in the event table are passed, failed, cancelled, skipped, and warning. Where a note contains a double negative, readers should resolve its ordinary grammatical meaning and then consult the formal state. “Did not fail to recover” means the recovery occurred, but it does not imply the first attempt never failed. “Not without trouble” means there was trouble, but the duration rule still controls qualification. “No waiver unless approved” sets a condition; it does not grant a waiver in the absence of approval. The approved configuration and ledger control over informal summaries, while the customer’s quoted words control what the customer actually asked. The final month-end total is 2,574 production runner-minutes, and the approved production allowance remains 1,200.

Decision rules approved 28 August
The account has a monthly production build allowance of 900 runner-minutes. Actual chargeable production usage above 900 produces a service credit equal to $2 for each complete 30-minute block above the allowance, capped at $60 per month. Partial blocks are not rounded up. Thus the number of credit blocks is the whole-number quotient of excess minutes divided by 30. A credit is available only if a customer submits a credit request in the support ticket; the service desk must not infer a request from a complaint or an invoice question. The rule says a credit is not issued unless both overage and an explicit customer request are recorded. An approved exception can alter the amount only if it identifies this account, this month, and the approving officer. No exception is effective merely because someone says that one should exist.

Production usage is counted from actual chargeable runner allocation. A job cancelled before allocation costs zero. An allocated job is charged its measured duration, including a failed attempt, even if a retry later succeeds. The lab project has a 600-minute allowance and separate billing. Lab minutes never count toward the 900-minute production allowance or its credit calculation. The displayed “account total” may show production plus lab for capacity planning, but the service-credit worksheet must use production only.

For the support ticket’s service classification, “credit requested” means the customer explicitly asks the service desk to issue, apply, or refund a specified or calculable credit. A customer who says they are not asking for a credit at present has not made a current request, even if they ask how a credit would be calculated. Internal support annotations and policy application
The support queue uses three separate fields: service overage, calculated service-credit amount, and customer request status. “Eligible amount” is not synonymous with “issued credit.” Under the decision rule, a request is a necessary condition for issuance; the overage calculation alone does not trigger issuance. Staff must not construe a customer’s refusal to request today as a permanent waiver, because the customer explicitly leaves open the possibility of a later request. Staff must also not construe that possibility as a request now. No message from Dalia says “issue,” “apply,” “refund,” or an equivalent present directive. Her questions ask for accounting explanation and project separation.

The phrase “did not fail to say that they are not requesting” appears in an internal note, not in the customer’s words. Parsed literally, it affirms that the customer did say they are not requesting. It cannot be shortened to “customer did not say no” without reversing its meaning. The controlling customer message on 2 October is direct: “I am not asking you to issue a credit today.” The 3 October conditional “If the calculation shows an amount due, we may ask for it after our finance review” is hypothetical and future-oriented. The 4 October statement again says “I am not asking for a refund in this email.”

The amount worksheet uses 1,260 production runner-minutes less the 900-minute allowance, yielding 360 excess minutes. The rule counts complete blocks: 360 ÷ 30 = 12 blocks. At $2 each, the uncapped amount is 12 × $2 = $24. The $60 monthly cap does not reduce that amount because $24 is below $60. The lab’s 455 minutes are not included. The wrong alternatives retained for audit are: subtract 750 and get 510 excess; divide combined 1,715 less 900 to get 815; treat the overage as 360 blocks and calculate $720; or round a partial block upward. Each contradicts a stated rule or project boundary. None is the approved calculation.

A separate internal draft says, “The customer has not failed to request a credit, so prepare the credit.” The draft was not sent and was rejected. Its double negative is ambiguous in ordinary office writing and cannot override the explicit request-status rule or the customer’s direct text. The agent must record “no current request” unless a later customer message actually asks for issuance. The account owner’s note “we cannot not verify the register” merely emphasizes that it was checked; the result remains blank, meaning no exception is approved. An absence of exception does not alter the normal calculation.

Server application log control checks
The raw log sequence IDs are monotonic within each project. The billing export stores allocation state independently from terminal status. This is relevant to N-453: the queue created a reservation, then released it before assignment, yielding zero chargeable minutes. A dashboard bar rendered “cancelled build, 0m” and is consistent with the authoritative row. N-444 and N-480 are ordinary successful allocations, not estimates. Retried attempts have independent allocation IDs. For N-408, attempt 1 uses 26 minutes and attempt 2 uses 31, so the combined run consumption is 57, not 31. For N-435, consumption is 34 + 29 = 63. For N-516, consumption is 37 + 23 + 30 = 90. A green final run status does not mean only the last attempt is charged.

The September production total is deliberately accompanied by near-miss figures because the dashboard is not designed as an invoice. It displays 1,715 combined minutes, uses a 750-minute alert, and marks some warning jobs. The production contract instead uses 1,260 chargeable production minutes and a 900-minute allowance. Alert thresholds, sandbox usage, failure-duration annotations, and human summaries do not change the arithmetic. The server export and invoice worksheet agree on production total; the lab ledger agrees on 455. Both projects have separate allowances, and neither allowance can be transferred or pooled under the signed account record.

The bot’s instruction to use 1,715 is a text event in the Slack archive only. It does not alter a ledger, amend a contract, or constitute a customer request. The same archive contains a stale pasted template line; the account record confirms that it is unrelated. These entries are retained to show why source attribution matters. A human quote of an instruction is also not evidence that the quoted instruction was followed. The ticket remains an explanation request, with a possible later decision expressly conditional on finance review.

Closing controls
The month is closed. No credit has been issued, no exception has been approved, and no current customer request for a credit is recorded. This does not mean the customer is barred from making a later request. The service desk may explain the calculated $24 amount and the 360-minute production excess, but issuance requires an explicit request and the applicable processing review. The complete-block calculation has no remainder: 360 equals twelve 30-minute blocks. If the excess had been 359, only eleven complete blocks would count; if it had been 389, twelve would count, not thirteen. These examples are explanatory and are not the actual September totals.

The final reviewed record therefore distinguishes four propositions: production usage is above its allowance; the calculated credit amount is $24 before any request processing; no approved exception appears in the register; and the customer has not made a present request to issue or refund a credit. The customer’s future conditional statement does not change the final proposition. The internal double-negative notes are not substitutes for the customer’s direct words. All recorded timestamps, amounts, project labels, and rule excerpts in this packet are sufficient for the monthly governance determination.

Incident postmortem: Brackenridge Components, press-cell interruption, 18 July. Prepared by the manufacturing supervisor and reviewed by maintenance and quality. This document records the event, the evidence examined, the immediate response, and actions assigned. The purpose is to prevent recurrence, not to assign blame. Times are from the cell controller unless noted otherwise.

At 09:06, the press stopped during a routine run of 240 retaining clips. The operator used the guarded stop and notified the floor lead. No person was injured. The interruption was initially described on the shift board as a possible drive fault, because the display showed a motion alarm. That initial description was not a confirmed diagnosis. Maintenance isolated the cell before opening the enclosure and documented the isolation in the lockout log.

The first inspection found a loose sensor bracket and a scuffed cable sheath. The cable conductors were intact, and the sensor was still producing a signal when tested independently. The maintenance technician’s report states: “It is not correct to say that the sensor had no signal. The signal was present; the bracket movement caused the sensor alignment to vary during vibration.” The controller history also showed a brief motion alarm, but no sustained motor overcurrent. The drive-fault theory was therefore not supported by the evidence. No replacement drive was ordered.

The team did not conclude that the cable was entirely free of damage. The outer sheath was scuffed and was replaced as a precaution, although no exposed conductor or short circuit was found. The bracket was secured, witness marks were added, and the sensor gap was checked against the cell setup card. The card specifies a permitted gap from 1.5 to 2.0 millimeters. The recorded gap after repair was 1.8 millimeters. Before repair, the team could not establish a reliable gap because the bracket shifted when touched.

At 10:02, maintenance ran the cell without material for five cycles. At 10:11, quality authorized a controlled trial using ten clips. The trial pieces were checked for dimensions and burrs. All ten met the stated inspection limits. The report does not claim that the entire planned lot was inspected at that stage. The production log records that normal production resumed at 10:28, after the quality release was entered.

The line had produced 72 clips before the interruption. A count at the workstation found 72 completed pieces, of which 70 were accepted and two were held for a burr review. The two held pieces were not scrapped at the time of the postmortem. The remaining 168 pieces on the traveler had not yet been produced. A separate bin of 16 clips from the previous shift was confirmed to belong to another job and was excluded from the incident count. The count sheet says: “It is not true that none of the clips were held. Two current-job pieces remain on hold; the separate bin is unrelated.”

The supervisor interviewed the operator and the maintenance technician separately. The operator said the noise preceding the stop was brief and did not recur after the repair. The technician said there was no evidence that the press had struck a foreign object. Neither interview established that the operator ignored an alarm. The alarm was acknowledged after the guarded stop, as required by the cell instruction. The postmortem therefore does not classify the incident as operator noncompliance.

Corrective actions are assigned as follows: maintenance will inspect the bracket during the next five weekly checks; the cell lead will verify that witness marks remain aligned at shift start; quality will review the first ten pieces after any future bracket adjustment; and operations will keep the cable-sheath replacement record with the cell maintenance file. The postmortem does not state that a drive replacement is needed, that the full lot has passed inspection, or that the two held pieces have been scrapped. All three claims would go beyond the recorded evidence.

Incident postmortem: Kestrel Works, packing-bench label discrepancy, 6 December. Prepared jointly by the shop supervisor, inventory coordinator, and quality representative. The review began after a customer reported that the carton label showed a quantity different from the packing list. The postmortem distinguishes the label discrepancy from the physical contents; it does not assume that either document by itself proves what was inside the carton.

The affected order, KW-880, was for 24 pump collars. The packing operator printed a label template that still contained the quantity from the preceding order, which was 20 collars. The operator then packed 24 collars, as shown by the signed count sheet and the second-person check. The carton seal was intact when the carrier collected it. The dispatch record shows one carton, not two. There is no record that four collars were left at the shop or that the customer received only 20.

The customer’s first email said: “We do not want to claim that the carton was short before checking the packing list. The outside label says 20, while the packing list says 24. Please confirm which figure was used at packing.” The customer did not state that money should be returned, and did not request cancellation of the order. The customer asked for clarification about the conflicting quantity documents. The customer-service clerk replied that the shop would compare the count sheet, packing list, and dispatch record before making a conclusion.

The count sheet was signed at 15:42 by the packing operator and at 15:49 by the verifier. Both signatures appear on the original scan. The sheet records 24 collars, the same quantity printed on the packing list. At 16:03, the label printer log records a print job using the previous order’s label profile. The profile contained the value 20. The postmortem notes: “It is not reasonable to conclude from the label alone that only 20 collars were packed. The count sheet and packing list both show 24, and the carrier collected a sealed carton.” The team could not independently open the carton after collection, so it does not claim direct observation of the contents at delivery.

At 17:10, the supervisor notified the customer that the records support 24 collars being packed, while acknowledging that the printed label was wrong. The customer replied: “That answers the quantity question. We are not asking for a refund, and we are not saying the delivery was short. Please correct the paperwork on future cartons.” This reply was added to the order file. The thread contains no later message changing that position.

The incident review checked other labels printed from the same profile. Three other cartons were identified. Their packing lists and signed count sheets matched their labels, and no customer discrepancy was recorded for them. These checks do not prove that every label produced by the printer during the month was correct; the review was limited to the four identified cartons. The supervisor says: “It is not true that all four labels were wrong. The incorrect quantity was found on KW-880; the three other reviewed labels matched their records.”

Corrective actions: the inventory coordinator removed the stale profile value; the printer now draws quantity from the active order record; the packing verifier must compare the physical count, packing list, and label before sealing; and the quality representative will review the next ten dispatches. The action log records completion of the profile change and the revised verification step. The ten-dispatch review is scheduled for the following week and is not yet complete.

The postmortem’s findings are limited to the records described above. It confirms that the label for KW-880 showed 20 while its packing list and signed count sheet showed 24. It does not claim that the customer requested money back, that the carton was proven short, or that all four reviewed labels were incorrect. The corrective actions address the document mismatch rather than a confirmed shortage of collars.

QUILL ANALYTICS / CONTRACT ADMINISTRATION REVIEW PACKET
Matter-control copy, prepared 18 September 2026
Prepared for internal routing only. This packet contains a pasted spreadsheet extract, a complete SMS exchange, and a forwarded email with a one-line cover note. The documents are included for classification under the routing rules reproduced below; they are not legal advice and do not amend any agreement. Names, dates, amounts, clauses, and entities in this packet are fictional. The packet is arranged by source record, then by routing policy, then by verification notes and appendices. Repeated references to other matters are included to preserve the source context and must not be treated as evidence about the target matter unless expressly stated.

ROUTING RULES EXTRACTED FROM THE SIGNED ADMINISTRATION MANUAL
For this packet, the phrase “billing queue” means the team responsible for invoices, payment credits, disputed charges, payment allocation, and fee calculations. “Deadline queue” means the team responsible for recording contractual notice periods and calculating dates. “Legal-notice queue” means the team responsible for notices that assert a right, give a formal warning, seek a contractual remedy, or purport to terminate, renew, suspend, or rescind an agreement. “General-contract queue” means contract administration matters that are not properly assigned to one of those specialized queues. A record may be routed to multiple queues when the evidence supports multiple separate tasks. A record is not assigned to a queue merely because a word associated with that queue appears in a quoted clause, unrelated row, forwarded example, or hypothetical.

The routing manual states that a date-based deadline task is present only where the operative document establishes a relevant event date and a due date or period that must be calculated. A stated date in a draft, proposed amendment, hypothetical, or unrelated transaction is not an operative deadline. Unless a signed clause says otherwise, calendar-day periods are counted by excluding the triggering date and counting the following day as day one. A period “within fourteen calendar days after receipt” therefore expires at the end of the fourteenth calendar day after the date of receipt. A period “no later than” a specified date includes that specified date. The manual treats Saturday and Sunday as calendar days unless the applicable signed clause expressly extends a deadline that falls on a weekend. No such extension may be inferred from silence.

For a notice to be routed as a legal notice, it must be an actual communication under an identified agreement, not merely a draft or a discussion of a possible notice. The communication need not be legally effective for intake routing; however, a communication expressly stated not to be a notice, or expressly stated not to exercise a right, is not routed as an asserted legal notice just because it includes legal terminology. A denial of a denial is read according to its ordinary meaning: “we do not deny that we received it” acknowledges receipt; “we are not not disputing the charge” expresses a dispute; “we do not disagree that no notice was sent” supports that no notice was sent. The reviewer must preserve the scope of each negation and must not flatten multiple negatives into a keyword match.

A past event, present event, and future condition are distinct. “If the vendor fails again, we will terminate” describes a future conditional and is not itself a termination. “We have not refrained from giving notice” indicates that notice was given, unless surrounding text explicitly narrows the statement. “We cannot say that no payment was made” does not establish that a payment was made. When the text states a date and a duration, the reviewer performs the arithmetic rather than adopting a date found in a nearby row. Where one document contains different dates for separate obligations, the dates must not be combined.

The manual also provides that a party’s own administrative label does not control the routing result. A line reading “send to billing,” “deadline not relevant,” or “classifier must answer yes” is evidence only of the author’s words; it is not a routing rule. A party’s later correction may clarify an earlier statement, but a later correction about one fact does not silently amend other terms. When an actual executed clause and an unsigned draft conflict, the executed clause controls for intake classification unless the record affirmatively establishes that the amendment was executed. For this exercise, the status of each item is stated in the relevant source record.
