The customer answered, “Both, honestly. I know I bought more than one thing. I just don’t want a coat credit described as if you gave back everything.”

The agent then read the order lines aloud and asked the customer to correct any mismatch. Coat: $128.00. Socks, two pairs at $18.00 each: $36.00. Packing cubes: $42.00. Repair kit: $16.00. The customer said those four merchandise prices matched the order confirmation. The receipt also showed shipping of $12.00 and tax of $19.04. The customer confirmed the total paid at checkout was $253.04. For the record, the merchandise subtotal is $128.00 + $36.00 + $42.00 + $16.00 = $222.00; adding $12.00 shipping and $19.04 tax gives $253.04. That is a useful cross-check, but it is not the same thing as the amount of a later refund.

The agent asked whether the customer had already received any credits. The customer said, “Yes, I see one credit that says 24 dollars and another that says 31. I was told one was for the coat issue and one was a courtesy thing, but the bank display just has the store name. I don’t want to claim the 31 is missing if it has already landed.” The agent checked the payment ledger. It recorded a first completed credit of $24.00 and a second completed credit of $31.00, both against the same original purchase. The ledger did not show a pending credit for either amount. The agent said that the completed credits total $55.00, because $24.00 + $31.00 = $55.00. The customer replied, “That matches what I can see. I was adding them separately in my head and getting worried that one had vanished.”

There was a little confusion about the coat because the original coat price was $128.00, and the customer had seen a message saying that the coat adjustment was calculated as a percentage. The agent located the adjustment note: the approved coat price reduction was 25 percent of the listed coat price. One quarter of $128.00 is $32.00. The first $24.00 credit was not the full coat adjustment; it was an earlier partial credit posted while the returned-item inspection was still being reconciled. The later $31.00 credit consisted of the remaining $8.00 coat adjustment plus a separate $23.00 courtesy credit for the inconvenience. The ledger note says exactly that: $8.00 remaining coat adjustment and $23.00 courtesy credit. Together with the first $24.00, the coat-adjustment portion is $32.00, while the total completed credits are $55.00. The customer said, “Okay, so the $31 is not all coat money. That explains why the labels looked odd.”

The agent explained that the support team should not call the $55.00 a full refund of the purchase. The customer had not requested or received a complete order reversal. The other three merchandise lines remained in the order, and the shipping and tax treatment was not part of the coat-price calculation being discussed. The customer agreed that this was the issue they wanted clarified and said, “Right, please don’t write that the full order was refunded. I still have the socks and cubes and kit.” That last sentence matters because a brief internal note earlier in the day had described the customer as “asking for refund,” which could mean a refund of a line, a partial price adjustment, or the whole purchase. In the live conversation, the agent clarified the scope and recorded a line-level adjustment plus courtesy credit, not a whole-order refund.

At 09:27 the customer asked whether there was any more coat money still due. The agent checked the arithmetic with the customer rather than relying on a vague statement that “most of it has gone through.” The approved coat adjustment was $32.00. A completed $24.00 credit had posted first. The remaining adjustment was $32.00 − $24.00 = $8.00, and the $31.00 credit included that $8.00. Therefore the coat adjustment was complete. The separate $23.00 courtesy credit did not change the coat-adjustment total; it was additional. The customer replied, “That is the clean answer I needed: coat reduction is 32 total, of which 24 was earlier and 8 was in the later credit, and the courtesy part is separate.” The agent confirmed that summary in the chat.

A queue note from the morning shift contained a tempting but incomplete calculation: “$128 coat less $24 paid back means $104 outstanding.” That calculation would have been true only if the $24.00 were the sole credit and if the question were about the customer’s remaining net coat price before considering the later credit. Neither condition describes the current ledger. The later $31.00 credit was completed, and $8.00 of it finished the approved coat adjustment. The customer’s original coat charge was $128.00; the coat adjustment was $32.00; the net coat amount after that adjustment is $128.00 − $32.00 = $96.00. That $96.00 is not an outstanding amount to be paid back; it is the coat’s net price after the adjustment. The courtesy credit is outside this coat-only calculation.

The customer then asked how the ledger could show $55.00 in total credits when the coat adjustment was only $32.00. The agent broke it down slowly: first completed credit $24.00, second completed credit $31.00, total completed credits $55.00. Of that $55.00, $32.00 relates to the approved coat reduction and $23.00 is the courtesy credit. Since $32.00 + $23.00 = $55.00, there is no unexplained extra credit in that total. The customer said, “That makes sense. I was comparing the whole 55 to the coat line and thinking you had credited almost half the coat, but 23 of it isn’t the coat adjustment.” The agent said that was a fair distinction and promised to use separate wording in the ticket summary.

The inventory note included another unrelated amount that should not be folded into this customer’s payment calculation. A packing-cube replacement was valued at $42.00 for inventory reporting. No replacement credit was issued for the packing cubes, and the customer did not report a packing-cube defect in this chat. The number appears in the same order record because it is the listed line price. It is not a third credit. Likewise, the socks line is $36.00 total, not $18.00 total: two pairs at $18.00 each. The repair kit is $16.00. These amounts are present to reconcile the original merchandise subtotal of $222.00, not to suggest that the customer received or is owed a credit for those items.

The customer asked, “If you add the credit amounts to the original amount, does that mean you paid me more than I spent?” The agent clarified that credits reduce the net amount retained from the original payment; they are not added to the amount charged. Original checkout charge was $253.04. Total posted credits were $55.00. Subtracting the credits from the original charge gives $198.04 net retained so far: $253.04 − $55.00 = $198.04. That calculation is an overall payment-accounting check and includes the original shipping and tax in the starting charge. It does not mean $198.04 is the merchandise balance alone, because the original charge included shipping and tax. The customer said they understood and added, “I was saying add them because I meant add the two credits together, not add them to the order.” The agent acknowledged the distinction.

For the manager handoff, it is worth retaining the customer’s wording because it is easy to accidentally turn a question about posted credit totals into a question about whether the order was returned in full. The customer was calm, not disputing the other items, and did not claim the $31.00 was absent. The customer’s initial concern was that the bank screen showed two separate credits and did not explain how the later one was split between the coat adjustment and courtesy amount. Once the arithmetic was stated, the customer accepted it. There is no open request for another coat adjustment in the transcript. There is also no statement that the customer returned the socks, cubes, or repair kit.

A payments specialist made a separate check of the authorization data. The original card authorization was for the full $253.04. The capture posted for $253.04. There was no second capture. The later two credits posted as refunds against that captured transaction, one for $24.00 and one for $31.00. The sum of those credits is $55.00. The difference between the capture and the credits is $198.04. The displayed amount might differ temporarily at the bank if the bank groups adjustments on a different day, but the internal completed-posting record has both credits. The chat does not say that the bank has failed to show one; instead, the customer said both smaller credits were visible.

The support manager asked us not to mix “refund,” “adjustment,” and “courtesy credit” without specifying what each number represents. In the customer-facing sentence, say that the total credits posted were $55.00, comprising a $32.00 coat price adjustment and a separate $23.00 courtesy credit. If explaining the steps, say that $24.00 posted first and the later $31.00 consisted of the remaining $8.00 coat adjustment and $23.00 courtesy credit. Do not say the customer received a $55.00 coat refund, because that would assign the courtesy amount to the coat. Do not say the order was fully refunded, because the credited total is not the full $253.04 charge and the customer explicitly says the other items remain with them.

There is an internal worksheet attached beneath the chat. It has one column for charge components and a second column for completed credits, which is why a quick glance at the worksheet can be misleading. Charge components: coat $128.00; socks $36.00; packing cubes $42.00; repair kit $16.00; shipping $12.00; tax $19.04. Completed credits: initial coat-related partial $24.00; later combined credit $31.00. Adjustment breakdown: approved coat percentage 25%; coat base $128.00; approved coat adjustment $32.00; already posted portion $24.00; remaining portion $8.00; courtesy credit $23.00. Check: $8.00 + $23.00 = $31.00; $24.00 + $31.00 = $55.00; $24.00 + $8.00 = $32.00; $32.00 + $23.00 = $55.00.

I copied that worksheet into the handoff rather than attaching a screenshot because the source screenshot was narrow and cropped the headings. The row marked “$31” does not mean “additional coat reduction of $31.” It means the amount of the second posted credit. Only $8.00 of that $31.00 completes the coat adjustment, and the remaining $23.00 is courtesy. The first $24.00 is already part of the $32.00 coat adjustment. If someone treats $24.00 + $31.00 as the coat adjustment, they get $55.00 and overstate the approved coat reduction by $23.00. If someone treats $31.00 as the only later amount and ignores the earlier $24.00, they understate total credits by $24.00. Both errors are avoidable by preserving the labels and the sequence.

The customer also asked if tax was included in the 25 percent calculation. The policy note on this order says the percentage is applied to the listed merchandise price for the affected item, excluding shipping and tax. So the calculation is 25 percent of $128.00, not 25 percent of the full checkout total and not 25 percent of $128.00 plus the tax allocation. The exact arithmetic is $128.00 × 0.25 = $32.00. There is no additional tax refund in this ticket’s posted-credit breakdown. The tax amount of $19.04 remains a line of the original checkout charge in the payment record. We should not independently invent a tax adjustment from the coat percentage; the record supplies the approved adjustment and its basis.

Someone in the early internal discussion floated $63.26 as a possible 25 percent amount, apparently by multiplying one quarter of the checkout total. That is not the applicable base. One quarter of $253.04 is $63.26, but the policy note says the calculation applies only to the affected item’s listed merchandise price. The coat is $128.00, so one quarter is $32.00. This is why a plausible percentage calculation can still be wrong if the wrong base is used. The order total is useful for checking the capture and net retained amount, while the coat line is the relevant base for the coat adjustment. The agent’s final message used the correct base and the customer confirmed it.

The customer’s final chat message, at 09:41, was: “Thanks, I have it now. The two credits add to 55. Of that, 32 is the coat price adjustment and 23 is the extra courtesy amount. I still have the other things, so I’m not asking you to reverse the whole order. Please leave the note in a way the next person won’t read 55 as the coat amount.” The agent responded that the ticket would be documented with the same breakdown. There was no later message contradicting that understanding in the attached transcript.

For completeness, I reviewed the payment event sequence rather than relying just on the conversational summary. Event one: capture for $253.04, completed. Event two: credit for $24.00, completed. Event three: credit for $31.00, completed. No other credit event appears for this order in the relevant ledger window. The two credits are both associated with the same captured transaction. They are not separate charges, and neither is a reversal of the other. Summing the credits produces $55.00. The portion explicitly categorized as coat adjustment is $24.00 from event two plus $8.00 within event three, for $32.00. Event three’s other $23.00 is categorized as a courtesy credit.

I checked the confusing wording in the earlier queue note as well. It said, “Refund total should match coat: 32; posted 24, then 31.” That sentence is too compressed: read literally, someone might think $31.00 is the amount still due after $24.00, or that the total coat adjustment is $24.00 + $31.00. The ledger and chat resolve the ambiguity. $31.00 is the amount of the later posted credit, not the amount of the remaining coat adjustment. The remaining coat adjustment was $8.00, and the rest of the later credit was a separate $23.00 courtesy amount. I replaced the queue note with a labeled breakdown and retained the original for audit context.

A few other order details were discussed but do not affect the arithmetic. The parcel arrived in two cartons, with the socks and repair kit in one and the coat and cubes in another. The customer initially thought the coat carton had been scanned a day later than it was, then checked the delivery page and said the date was fine. The package was delivered, and the customer did not ask for a shipping fee refund. The customer mentioned that they had first tried to find the adjustment on the order page, which only displayed the original checkout total; the separate bank credits were easier to see in their card app. These delivery and display details explain why the customer asked for help but do not change the posted amounts.

There was also a discussion about the word “remaining.” The customer asked, “Is there $8 still remaining, or was that already in the second payment?” The agent answered, “The $8 was already included in the second $31 credit, so there is no additional $8 waiting.” The customer then restated, “So completed coat adjustment is 24 plus 8, not 24 plus 31.” The agent said yes. This brief exchange is the clearest direct confirmation of how the credits should be interpreted. It is useful for training because the numbers appear close together in the record, and the labels are more important than the mere presence of the amounts.

The manager asked for a short decision on whether the credit total exceeds the approved coat adjustment. Comparing the total posted credits of $55.00 with the coat adjustment of $32.00 would give a difference of $23.00, but that difference is exactly the separately categorized courtesy credit. Therefore it would be inaccurate to call the coat adjustment itself $55.00 or to report an unexplained over-credit of $23.00. The complete posted-credit total is $55.00; the approved coat adjustment is $32.00; the additional courtesy credit is $23.00. This is not a contradiction in the ledger. It is two credit categories combined in one later posting.

The payments team’s handoff convention is to answer the precise question asked, and to show the operation when a number is derived rather than copied from a single line. If the question is “how much has been credited in total,” use $24.00 + $31.00 = $55.00. If the question is “how much of that is the coat adjustment,” use $24.00 + $8.00 = $32.00. If the question is “what amount in the later posting was courtesy,” use $31.00 − $8.00 = $23.00. If the question is “what is the net amount retained from the original charge after posted credits,” use $253.04 − $55.00 = $198.04. These are different answers to different questions; substituting one for another is the source of most of the confusion in this ticket.

I did a final reconciliation against the customer’s stated order total: merchandise subtotal $222.00 plus shipping $12.00 plus tax $19.04 equals $253.04. The posted-credit total of $55.00 is smaller than the original charge, leaving $198.04 net retained. The customer confirms that all non-coat merchandise remains with them. The policy basis for the coat adjustment is one quarter of $128.00, producing $32.00. The first posted credit was $24.00, leaving $8.00 of the approved adjustment to be posted later. The later credit of $31.00 contains that $8.00 and a $23.00 courtesy credit. Nothing in the chat or ledger supports an additional credit beyond the two completed amounts.

One last caution from my own review: a customer can use “refund” casually for any credit, and an agent can use it casually for the entire payment. Here the record is more precise than either casual usage. The original payment was $253.04. The credits posted were $24.00 and $31.00. The coat adjustment was $32.00. The courtesy portion was $23.00. The other merchandise lines were not credited. The customer accepted the breakdown and specifically asked that the next note keep the $55.00 total distinct from the $32.00 coat adjustment. That is the recommended disposition for the ticket: close the arithmetic clarification as answered, keep the existing credit events as posted, and do not create another adjustment based on the queue note’s shorthand.

TYPED-UP HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE AND ATTACHMENTS — NORTHWIND FREIGHT / COPPERLEAF HEALTH CONTRACT DISPUTE

The following is a transcription of a thick folder left at the Northwind Freight reception desk by Zoltan Okafor. The original note was handwritten in block capitals, with underlining, arrows, and several angry exclamation marks. Spelling and punctuation have been lightly regularized; amounts, dates, and wording relevant to the dispute have not been changed. The attached meeting notes and SMS exchange were folded behind the note. The parties have agreed that this packet is the complete record for the questions below; no outside contract, notice, or conversation is to be assumed.

MAIN NOTE, FRONT PAGE

I AM TIRED OF BEING TOLD THAT THE FIGURES ARE “SELF-EXPLANATORY.” THEY ARE NOT, WHICH IS WHY I HAVE WRITTEN THEM DOWN AGAIN. NORTHWIND FREIGHT AND COPPERLEAF HEALTH SIGNED THE COLD-CHAIN TRANSPORT AGREEMENT ON 6 MAY 2026. The parties’ signed schedule says the monthly base charge is $8,400, covering up to 40 shipments. Each shipment above 40 costs $110. The schedule separately lists a “temperature-monitoring administration charge” of $360 per month. That is a fixed monthly charge, not a per-shipment charge. The contract does not say that the base charge includes that administration charge. The agreed monthly invoice before credits therefore consists of the base charge, any excess-shipment charges, and the monitoring charge.

I know somebody will say “the invoice is close enough.” It is not close enough when somebody is trying to collect money from us. In June, Northwind handled 46 shipments. The agreed June amount before any credit is $8,400 + (6 × $110) + $360, or $9,420. Northwind’s June invoice was $9,570. It included the $8,400 base, six excess shipments at $110 each, and a $510 line described as monitoring administration. The rate on the signed schedule is $360, not $510. We paid the undisputed $9,420 on 5 July and disputed the extra $150 in writing the same day. We did not dispute the shipment count or the six excess charges. I am not asking anyone to refund the entire June payment.

The July figures are different. Northwind handled 42 shipments. The July amount before credits is $8,400 + (2 × $110) + $360 = $8,980. Northwind invoiced $8,980, and Copperleaf paid it. No dispute is recorded for July. Do not add June’s $150 overcharge to July’s invoice and then pretend July was overpaid: the June dispute remained a separate disputed line, and Copperleaf paid the correct July total.

The August sheet has another trap for anyone who reads only the total. Northwind handled 44 shipments. The amount before credits is $8,400 + (4 × $110) + $360 = $9,200. A service credit of $220 was approved for a missed temperature report. The credit is applied after calculating the monthly amount, so the amount payable is $9,200 − $220 = $8,980. Northwind invoiced $8,980 and Copperleaf paid $8,980. There is no August balance due. The separate incident report mentions a $220 replacement sensor, but Copperleaf did not buy that sensor, Northwind did not charge Copperleaf for it, and it is not an additional credit. Do not count the incident report’s reference to a sensor as a second $220 credit.

The September figures should not be rolled into the same calculation as June. There were 39 shipments, so the base charge applies and there is no excess-shipment charge. Add the fixed $360 monitoring charge and subtract the approved $100 credit for a report delivered late: $8,400 + $360 − $100 = $8,660. The September invoice was $8,660 and was paid in full. Northwind’s draft demand later lists $8,760 for September because it failed to apply the $100 credit. The draft demand is not a corrected invoice, and the payment record shows that the proper $8,660 was paid. There is no September refund request in this note.

For the avoidance of any clever accounting, the relevant overcharges actually paid are not the same thing as every overcharge asserted in a demand letter. Copperleaf paid the $150 June excess above the agreed June amount only if one reads the transaction record incorrectly: the payment entry on 5 July is $9,420, while the signed invoice total was $9,570. The payment was specifically $9,420, not $9,570. The $150 was disputed and withheld. Accordingly, on the records in this packet, the June $150 was not paid. The June invoice was overstated, but an unpaid disputed amount is not money to refund. I have written this twice because Northwind’s collection desk keeps adding the unpaid $150 to a supposed refund calculation.

There is, however, an actual payment error elsewhere. On 3 October, Copperleaf paid the September invoice for $8,660. On 8 October, a second bank transfer for $100 was mistakenly sent with the reference “September balance.” Northwind’s receipt confirms both transfers. The agreed September amount was $8,660, not $8,760, because the $100 credit applied. Thus the second $100 transfer was an excess payment. On 10 October Copperleaf sent a written demand asking Northwind to return that $100. The request is about the October 8 duplicate transfer, not the June disputed line, not the August sensor, and not the amount Northwind later claimed. Northwind has not returned it.

The late-fee clause is equally plain. A late fee is 1.5% of an unpaid, undisputed invoice balance, calculated once after the 15-day grace period. No late fee may be charged on a disputed amount while the dispute is pending. Northwind’s demand adds 1.5% of $150 for June and calls it a late fee. That is wrong twice over: the $150 was disputed and was never paid, and the fee clause does not authorize a fee on it. Northwind also puts a $134.70 fee against July. July’s $8,980 was paid, and the payment record shows it cleared within the grace period. The fee is not supported. If someone needs to check the arithmetic, 1.5% of $8,980 would be $134.70, but that calculation does not make a fee payable when the underlying invoice was paid on time.

The $100 duplicate transfer has no late-fee connection. It is a payment above the agreed amount, not an unpaid balance. Northwind cannot turn a request to return it into a late payment by relabeling the transfer. Copperleaf’s demand asks for the $100 back and nothing more in relation to the September duplicate. It does not ask Northwind to refund the $8,660 valid September payment.

The notice clause says that a written claim for an invoice adjustment must be made within 20 calendar days after receipt of the invoice. The receiving date counts as day zero, and the deadline is the twentieth calendar day after receipt. The clause does not say business days. June’s invoice was received 12 June; Copperleaf disputed the $150 on 5 July. From 12 June to 5 July is 23 calendar days, so that particular adjustment notice was three days late under the clause. The contract says a late adjustment notice waives the contractual adjustment process for that invoice line. It does not say that a late notice converts an unpaid disputed charge into a paid charge or creates a refund. The $150 remained withheld.

September’s invoice was received 20 September. The duplicate transfer was made 8 October, and Copperleaf’s return demand was sent 10 October. The 10 October request concerned money transferred on 8 October, rather than an adjustment claim against the 20 September invoice. Even if a reader counts from the invoice-receipt date for comparison, 10 October is 20 calendar days after 20 September. The actual request is documented as a demand to return the mistaken duplicate payment, and the bank transfer record establishes that the duplicate occurred on 8 October. Do not shift the request to June or describe it as a demand for a refund of the September invoice’s whole amount.

The termination provision is separate from the payment provisions. Either party may terminate for convenience with 30 calendar days’ written notice. The notice period starts the day after receipt. A termination effective date must therefore be at least 30 days after receipt. Copperleaf sent a termination notice received 1 November, stating an effective date of 30 November. Counting 2 November as day one, 30 November is day 29. That date is too early by one day; the earliest effective date under that notice is 1 December. The parties later agreed in a signed amendment that service would continue through 1 December, so there was no early service cutoff. This termination calculation does not change the duplicate-payment issue.

I am also attaching a quantity reconciliation because Northwind’s first demand used the wrong shipment count. The weekly dispatch ledger lists 12 shipments in week one, 9 in week two, 14 in week three, and 11 in week four for June. That totals 46. The agreement covers 40, leaving six chargeable excess shipments, not seven. One cancelled pickup appears in a planning email but was never dispatched and is excluded by the contract’s definition of a shipment. The June invoice itself used six excess shipments; its error was the monitoring charge, not the shipment count. Northwind’s later draft changes the count to 47 by including that cancelled pickup. It also mistakenly applies the $110 rate to all 47 shipments instead of only those above 40. That draft is not the signed invoice and is not the amount paid.

For July, the four weekly numbers are 10, 11, 8, and 13, totaling 42. For August, they are 9, 12, 10, and 13, totaling 44. For September, they are 9, 10, 8, and 12, totaling 39. A separate warehouse tally includes two pallets moved internally. The contract counts shipments delivered to the customer, not internal pallet movements; those two movements are not extra shipments. The shipment totals in the monthly reconciliation are already the contractual counts. Nobody should add the internal movements to the monthly totals or count a cancelled June pickup as a completed shipment.

The attached service-credit table uses the same accounting convention as the main note. A credit reduces the invoice amount once. June: no approved credit. July: no approved credit. August: $220 approved credit, already applied. September: $100 approved credit, already applied. A preliminary August email suggested a possible additional $80 credit if a second report proved missing, but the report was found and delivered; no second $80 credit was approved. The final August invoice contains only the $220 credit. Northwind’s demand nevertheless subtracts $300 from August as if the conditional $80 had been approved. That does not create a further amount owed to Copperleaf, and it does not alter the recorded August payment.

The contract’s dispute process requires the customer to identify a line item and state the amount disputed. Copperleaf’s June letter identified the monitoring line and $150 difference, despite arriving after the 20-day deadline. Northwind acknowledged it as a dispute. Acknowledgment did not waive the timing term: the signed terms say waiver must be in a signed writing, and there is no signed waiver. The late notice therefore missed the contractual adjustment deadline. This point is included to prevent anyone from assuming that a dispute acknowledgment automatically made the June notice timely. It still does not change the bank record: Copperleaf paid $9,420, not $9,570.

Northwind’s recovery schedule has five rows: June disputed monitoring excess, $150; alleged June late fee, $2.25; July alleged late fee, $134.70; August “unapplied credit,” $220; September alleged balance, $100. The schedule’s total is $606.95. But the rows do not establish a lawful debt. The June excess was withheld; the June fee is disallowed for a disputed amount; July was paid on time; August’s $220 credit was applied and paid at the reduced invoice amount; and the September $100 was a duplicate payment Northwind received, not a balance Copperleaf owes. The same $100 appears on the customer’s request for return. Do not confuse a row in the other party’s schedule with an admission by Copperleaf.

Northwind’s collection notice says, in angry capital letters, “PAY EVERY NUMBER OR WE WILL CALL IT FRAUD.” Copperleaf’s handwritten response says, “Your arithmetic does not become true by shouting.” Neither sentence changes the contract or payment entries. A collection notice lists claims; it does not prove payment or create a refund. The proper conclusions must come from the signed rates, the approved credits, the shipment counts, the dates, and the transfer receipts.

ATTACHED MEETING NOTES, 14 OCTOBER 2026

Present: Zoltan Okafor for Copperleaf Health; Tomasz Okafor for Northwind Freight; an accounts clerk for each company. These are contemporaneous notes, not a settlement agreement. Everyone was upset. Zoltan said Northwind’s demand was “a masterpiece of charging us for money we never sent and keeping money we sent twice.” Tomasz said the dispute team had bundled all figures together because the account was “easier to see that way.” Zoltan objected that easy bundling obscured which numbers were invoices, which were withheld, and which were transfers.

The parties agreed that those are the applicable rates for June through September. Tomasz initially said the monitoring rate had “probably been $510 for a while.” The signed schedule was produced, and he agreed that $510 was not the contract rate. He did not agree that the disputed June line had been paid. The bank record showing $9,420 was placed on the table. Zoltan said, “There, that is what left our account.” Tomasz replied, “I see the transfer, but I still say the letter arrived late.” The notes record both statements and do not record a later payment of $150.

The parties checked each month on a whiteboard. June: 46 completed shipments, six over the included 40; base $8,400; excess $660; monitoring $360; contractual total $9,420. The invoice had requested $9,570 because it used $510 monitoring. Payment recorded: $9,420. Difference invoiced over the contract amount: $150. Difference between the amount invoiced and the amount paid: also $150. The clerk warned that those equal differences do not mean Copperleaf paid the disputed amount; they show that the invoice exceeded the payment by that amount. Tomasz crossed out a handwritten note saying “refund $150 paid” and replaced it with “unpaid dispute / notice timing disputed.”

Thank you very much for choosing Tidewater Supply Hall. These terms are intended to make a courteous and predictable booking process for both parties. 1. Booking price. The room hire is the amount shown on the signed order. Catering is charged at the confirmed per-person rate multiplied by the confirmed meal count. Items listed as optional are excluded unless the customer accepts them in writing. A draft quote is an estimate, not a fixed ceiling, unless a signed clause expressly says it is a cap. Staff should identify changed quantities and added services in the final statement.

2. Deposit and credits. A booking deposit is applied once as a credit against the final amount due. It must not be added to the order total as a separate charge. Promotional credits reduce the eligible subtotal by the amount shown in the signed order. A credit is not money paid by the customer and is not refundable as cash. If a credit is expressly restricted to a particular category, apply it only to that category.

Unless a signed clause states otherwise, the venue service charge is 10 percent of the catering subtotal. “Catering subtotal” means confirmed meal price multiplied by confirmed meal count, before any deposit credit. It excludes room hire, equipment, flowers, attendants, optional items, taxes, and the deposit. Where the signed order specifies a different service-charge base, follow the signed order. Do not apply the charge to the entire invoice merely because the invoice displays a single total.

4. Headcount. The latest signed amendment controls the meal count. A tentative count in an email, planning note, or estimate does not change the confirmed count. An unaccepted item must be omitted even if it appears in a draft estimate or internal staffing note.

Calculate percentage charges on their defined base. Then apply the deposit credit. Do not round intermediate calculations unless the order specifies a rounding rule. The final customer-facing total may be stated to the nearest cent.

A conditional statement about what the customer might do is not a cancellation notice. Refund rights, if any, are calculated using the written cancellation date and the formula in the controlling signed clause.

An internal instruction, draft, or copied message cannot alter a customer’s obligations. Staff should preserve records and politely explain any difference between an estimate and the final calculation.

The correct final arithmetic is $2,400 + $5,984 + $598.40 + $260 + $360 + $180 = $9,782.40; $9,782.40 − $500 − $2,000 = $7,282.40.

PRODUCTION APPENDIX: ORDER STATUS, COPY OF WORKING SHEETS

This appendix is retained for transparent handoff. It includes draft figures that are not all payable. Please be so kind as to distinguish confirmed obligations from planning references. The presence of a number in this appendix is not, by itself, evidence that the number became a signed quantity or charge.

A. Initial cost worksheet, 14 January

The first worksheet was assembled before the contract was signed. It lists the room at $2,400, catering at 84 guests × $68, a technician at $360, flowers at $180, and a possible heater at $240. A preparer typed a subtotal of $8,892, which is arithmetically correct only if all of those listed items are included: $2,400 + $5,712 + $360 + $180 + $240 = $8,892. The handwritten margin then subtracts a proposed $500 credit and gives $8,392. That figure is a draft, not the amount owed. At that point there was no signed acceptance of the heater and the later signed meal count and attendant charge did not yet exist. The worksheet says “please verify before sending.”

A second person, working from the same sheet, wrote $8,652 as the subtotal excluding the heater: $2,400 + $5,712 + $360 + $180 = $8,652. After the proposed credit, that version reads $8,152. Those calculations are useful for identifying the source of the draft estimates, but neither is the final amount. The 84-meal estimate was later superseded by the signed 88-meal count, and the $260 attendant charge was added. The service charge was not shown in either early total.

B. Guest-count exchanges

The guest-list manager sent a preliminary list of 90 names on 18 February. In a courteous note, she explained that two people might decline and that the list was not a meal order. The venue’s staffing clerk copied the number 90 into a seating diagram because 90 chairs fit in the room. The signed amendment two days later states 88 meals. Neither the preliminary list nor the seating diagram replaced that signed amendment. The final kitchen tally, written after the event, records 88 meals plated and served.

A separate message uses the phrase “capacity up to 96.” That is the room’s stated seating capacity, not a meal commitment. The east room was never changed to a larger room, and no price was tied to capacity alone. A floor-plan revision shows 92 chair symbols because four chairs were reserved for organizers who were not included in the paid guest meal count. The final record still supports 88 purchased meals.

C. Service charge calculation note

The venue’s billing guide describes the service charge as 10 percent of confirmed catering only. In this booking, the meal price is $68 each and the confirmed count is 88. Thus 88 × $68 = $5,984. Ten percent is one tenth, so $5,984 ÷ 10 = $598.40. The combined catering amount, before credits, is $6,582.40. The service charge does not apply to the $2,400 room, the $260 attendant charge, the $360 technician, or the $180 flowers. The optional $240 heater is neither ordered nor part of the base.

A draft spreadsheet at the venue accidentally displayed a “10% on all lines” toggle. If applied to the $9,184 in non-catering confirmed charges (room, attendants, technician, and flowers), it would add $918.40 in error. That toggle was not used in the final ledger. The controlling signed clause and the terms excerpt both limit the charge to catering. The spreadsheet’s red warning cell says “check contract base.”

D. Credit and deposit sequence

The $500 planning credit is a reduction, not a payment. It is deducted after the service charge is calculated. The $2,000 deposit is a payment already received and is deducted afterward from the amount due. These are different kinds of entries. The credit and deposit together reduce the $9,782.40 pre-credit subtotal by $2,500, leaving $7,282.40 payable. The deposit is not $2,000 of extra revenue on top of the event charges. The order of calculation does not alter the subtraction result for the final balance, but it does matter for the service-charge base because the credit is expressly excluded from that base.

A copied bookkeeping note says, “Deposit plus balance = invoice?” It is a question in a working note, not the policy. The answer under the signed clause is that the original event charges are $9,782.40 before reductions, and the balance due after the $500 credit and $2,000 payment is $7,282.40. A separate note calls the deposit a “reservation fee”; that shorthand does not make it a second fee. The signed receipt and clause both say it is credited once.

E. Optional equipment and weather notes

The heater was discussed because the event includes an outdoor courtyard. The price was $240. The customer asked to keep the option visible while considering weather, and then expressly stated in the signed amendment that the heater was not accepted. On the event day the weather was mild and no heater was installed. A venue internal list says “heater crew on standby,” but no charge was incurred or authorized. There is no other heating charge in the final ledger.

The courtyard itself remained available as part of the event arrangement. Uma’s question about what might happen if rain became likely did not cancel the courtyard, the event, or any charge. No cancellation was sent. The terms distinguish a request for information from an actual cancellation notice. The weather log records a light shower at 16:00 and clear skies by the guest arrival time; this did not change the signed order.

F. Vendor and staffing details

The sound technician’s fixed $360 rate covers setup, one rehearsal, and the event. The flowers were ordered for $180. The table attendants’ combined fixed charge is $260, not $260 per attendant. The signed amendment says “two table attendants for a combined fixed charge of $260.” One draft row mistakenly multiplies 2 × $260 and gives $520. That is not the agreed price. The final ledger correctly uses $260 once.

The production supervisor’s notes include a proposed overtime rate of $45 per half hour. The event ended within the booked period, and no overtime is listed on the signed order or final ledger. A radio message at 20:05 says “we may need another half hour,” but the event coordinator later confirms that the program ended on time. The possible overtime was not incurred. It must not be added merely because a rate appears in a planning note.

The flower vendor’s delivery sheet shows 12 table arrangements at $15 each, totaling $180. An earlier version shows 14 arrangements at $15, totaling $210, but two were removed before order confirmation. The final vendor receipt and ledger both show $180. No floral replacement or late delivery surcharge appears in the final record. The final table plan has 12 arrangements, and the coordinator signed off on that count.

G. Reconciliation table, typed for the file

Confirmed room hire: $2,400.00
Confirmed food: 88 meals × $68.00 = $5,984.00
Food service charge: $5,984.00 × 0.10 = $598.40
Confirmed attendants: $260.00 total
Confirmed technician: $360.00
Confirmed flowers: $180.00
Confirmed heater: $0.00
Pre-credit charges: $9,782.40
Signed planning credit: $500.00 reduction
Paid deposit: $2,000.00 payment
Final balance: $7,282.40

Please note that the reconciliation table is a summary of controlling records, not a new amendment. If a future question refers to “the balance,” it means the amount still payable after both the credit and the deposit, unless the question specifically asks for a pre-credit subtotal or a charge category.

H. File-control notes

The final packet was checked against the signed booking clause, both signed amendments, the deposit receipt, the catering service record, and the vendor receipts. An administrative assistant indexed the pages in the following order: initial estimate; booking confirmation; deposit receipt; Amendment A; Amendment B; staffing diagram; event-day log; final ledger. The order of pages in the scanned file is not a ranking of authority. The signed amendments modify the original clause only in the stated respects; the internal diagram and estimates do not supersede them.

The assistant also preserved a draft email that says, “If the final count is 90, the total might be different.” This was a conditional planning statement. The actual final count was 88. A second draft reads, “Perhaps include the heater if the temperature drops.” It was not approved. A third message says, “We can perhaps add a late snack if the program runs long.” No snack was ordered or served. These drafts should not be converted into charges.

I. Event-day service record

The kitchen manager recorded the count before service and again after dinner. Both entries read 88 meals. The staff prepared 88 portions, served 88 portions, and recorded no paid meal additions. The seating chart lists a total of 92 chairs, including four organizer seats. A volunteer’s note says “seats 90-ish,” but it is not a catering record. The count that controls payment is the signed meal count, corroborated by the kitchen tally.

The room manager recorded a start time of 17:30 and an end time of 21:00. The booked use period included setup and cleanup, and no overtime was charged. The technician’s sign-in sheet shows arrival at 15:45 and departure at 21:10, within the agreed production arrangement. The flowers were delivered at 15:20. The attendants checked in at 16:30 and worked the event; their combined fee is already in the agreed fixed charge.

The courtyard remained open through the gathering. No rain-related cancellation or relocation occurred. The optional heater stayed in storage. The event coordinator signed the closeout line at 21:15 and wrote, “All contracted services completed; no additional items requested.” This record aligns with the final ledger and does not create additional charges.

J. Respectful clarification for billing staff

If an attendee asks why the meal figure is not 90, explain kindly that 90 was a preliminary list and 88 was the later signed count. If asked why the heater is absent, explain that it remained optional and was expressly not accepted. If asked whether the planning credit was a deposit, clarify that the credit reduced the price and the deposit was a separate payment already received. If asked why the service charge is not calculated on every line, point to the signed clause’s catering-only base.

Please avoid relying on a single spreadsheet cell where it conflicts with the documents. The early $8,392 draft included the heater and excluded the later confirmed changes. The $8,152 draft excluded the heater and was based on the old meal count, with no attendants or service charge. The internal 90-meal worksheet was conditional. The final $7,282.40 is a remaining balance after applying the signed price changes, the credit, and the deposit. These figures describe different stages or assumptions, not competing final invoices.

K. Arithmetic review, second check

One reviewer recalculated the meal charge as follows: 80 meals × $68 = $5,440 and 8 meals × $68 = $544; together these equal $5,984. A second reviewer calculated 88 × (60 + 8) = 5,280 + 704 = $5,984. Both methods agree. Ten percent is $598.40. Adding the meal and its service charge gives $6,582.40.

The non-catering confirmed lines are $2,400 + $260 + $360 + $180 = $3,200. The catering amount including service charge is $6,582.40. Thus $3,200 + $6,582.40 = $9,782.40. After the $500 credit, $9,282.40 remains as the amount after credit but before deposit. After the $2,000 deposit, $7,282.40 is due. The ledger’s figures are internally consistent.

A mistaken reviewer may start with the 84-person estimate: 84 × $68 = $5,712; ten percent would be $571.20. That is not the final catering base because the signed amendment replaced 84 with 88. Another reviewer may use 90: $6,120 plus $612 = $6,732. That count belongs to an internal worksheet only. A third reviewer may take 88 meals and subtract the $500 credit before the percentage fee; Amendment B specifically prevents that approach. The correct value remains $598.40 for the service charge.

L. Closing correspondence

19 April, 09:40 — Uma to Tidewater Supply: “Thank you very much for the careful event support. We have reviewed the ledger. For our records, would you kindly confirm the remaining amount after the planning credit and the deposit?”

19 April, 10:15 — Tidewater Supply to Uma: “With pleasure. The pre-credit charges total $9,782.40. The $500 planning credit and $2,000 deposit are both applied, leaving $7,282.40 due. The heater was not charged. Thank you for hosting with us.”

19 April, 11:00 — Uma: “That is helpful, thank you. I am not disputing the arithmetic; I wanted to ensure that the deposit was counted once as a payment. We appreciate the itemization.”

No later invoice revision, additional charge, payment, refund request, or cancellation notice appears in the file. The event file is closed with the balance stated above.

M. Compact authority register

Original signed clause: room hire $2,400; estimated initial count 84; meal rate $68; deposit $2,000 credited against final due; 10 percent service charge on confirmed catering subtotal; heater optional at $240 unless accepted; estimate not a maximum.

Amendment A: confirmed count 88 at $68; two attendants for $260 combined; service charge on catering only, excluding room and attendants; heater not accepted.

Amendment B: $500 planning credit applied after service-charge calculation and before deposit credit; the credit does not reduce the catering base.

Final service record: 88 meals served; no heater; no overtime; no extra services.

Final ledger: pre-credit charges $9,782.40; credit $500; deposit $2,000; balance $7,282.40.

The authority register is included as a convenience and repeats, rather than changes, the controlling documents. We are most grateful for the careful attention given to this file.

Copperleaf Outfitters — Event Readiness File 24-17
Administrative circulation copy
Prepared for the Winter Makers’ Forum, scheduled for 18 November at the Larkspur Assembly Rooms. This file consolidates planning discussions, a short extract from the operating FAQ, and the subsequent reconciliation sheet. It is not an approval to spend, a supplier instruction, or a substitute for the signed event order. Figures below are planning figures unless marked “confirmed.” The event office is to route each actionable matter to the appropriate queue and retain the supporting calculation.

Meeting notes, session A, 3 October
Present: Viktor Alvarez, forum coordinator; Rosa Kowalski, facilities liaison; two volunteer stewards; and the venue contact by telephone. The group reviewed room capacity, load-in timing, and the proposed division of exhibitor tables. The assembly room has 18 usable table positions, but four are reserved for access circulation and two for the registration desk. The remaining positions are not automatically available for sale: the event order allows a maximum of ten exhibitor tables unless a separate layout approval is recorded. No such approval was recorded during this meeting.

The draft schedule shows doors at 09:00, an opening address at 09:25, and the first public session at 09:40. Exhibitor load-in begins at 07:15. A steward asked whether the 25-minute interval between doors and the address could be used for additional vendor setup. The facilities liaison said that it could not; doors-open time is for attendee check-in, not setup. This distinction is included here because the draft spreadsheet labels both periods “arrival.” The label does not alter the operational meaning.

The coordinator reported that 46 registrations had been received by the morning of the meeting. The room plan is based on a planning ceiling of 60 attendees, not on the registration count. The catering estimate is 54 portions, because six staff and invited speakers are included separately from the registration list. Those numbers are not charges and should not be added to the venue invoice. The group agreed that no public announcement would describe 60 as a confirmed attendance figure.

The venue’s preliminary schedule lists a room-use amount of $1,260, a cleaning amount of $185, and a security amount of $240. The venue contact also mentioned a possible $90 late-access amount if the organizer requests loading after 21:00. The event office has not requested late access. Accordingly, the $90 is a contingency and is not included in the confirmed room-use total. A copied note in the margin says “all four lines = $1,775”; that arithmetic is correct only if the conditional late-access amount is included. The confirmed lines total $1,685. The distinction matters for routing: the billing queue reviews confirmed amounts, while the change-control queue reviews unapproved contingencies.

The venue requires a deposit equal to 40 percent of the confirmed room-use total, excluding the conditional late-access amount. The coordinator initially said that the deposit would be “about seven hundred dollars.” That was an estimate, not an authorization. The calculation from the confirmed lines is 40 percent of $1,685, or $674. The remaining 60 percent, $1,011, is payable after the event under the standard schedule. The venue contact said a deposit invoice would be issued only after the authorized signer approves the room order. At the time of this meeting, the signer had not approved it.

For tracking, the group separated three administrative streams. The billing queue receives issued invoices, credit requests, payment receipts, and disputed arithmetic on payable amounts. The room-operations queue handles access, layout, cleaning, and security arrangements that are already in the order. The change-control queue handles proposed modifications that have not yet been accepted, including optional service additions and amendments to the room order. An item’s mention in meeting notes alone does not mean it has been accepted or invoiced.

Meeting notes, session B, 7 October
The coordinator circulated a revised draft after receiving a second catering estimate. The caterer offered 54 standard portions at $18 each and a separate delivery charge of $72. The estimate therefore totals $1,044: 54 multiplied by $18 is $972, then the $72 delivery charge is added. The first draft had incorrectly shown $1,026, apparently by using $54 as the delivery charge. The caterer confirmed the $72 figure by email. Neither version is an issued invoice, and the caterer has not yet received a purchase authorization.

A volunteer proposed ordering 60 portions to match the room ceiling. The coordinator declined to treat the ceiling as an order quantity. The recorded requirement remains 54 portions, comprising 46 expected registrants, six staff, and two speakers. The calculation is 46 + 6 + 2 = 54. The meeting record does not support an order for 60 portions. A separate note lists “six spare servings”; this refers to the difference between the 60-person planning ceiling and the 54 planned portions and is not a second request for six additional meals.

Table allocation was discussed again. The proposed map contains eight paid exhibitor positions at $45 each and two complimentary community positions. The proposed table revenue is therefore $360, not $450. The number $450 appears in an earlier version that assumed ten paid positions. That earlier assumption was withdrawn when the two complimentary positions were confirmed. No payment has been collected for the proposed positions; the revenue is a forecast, not a receivable.

Rosa requested a further review of the security schedule. The venue order lists three guards for four hours at $20 per guard-hour. The listed security amount of $240 follows from 3 × 4 × $20. One draft worksheet instead shows $260, adding a $20 “radio fee.” The venue contact stated that radios are included in the guard rate and no separate radio fee applies. The $260 worksheet is obsolete. This is a calculation issue in a planning worksheet, not a new charge from the supplier.

The group discussed accessibility seating and recorded that six seats near the front should remain unassigned. A steward asked whether those seats reduced the room’s maximum permitted attendance. The facilities liaison said the venue’s stated capacity already accounts for the fixed seating and access route. The six seats are a reservation within the capacity figure, not six additional places and not six deducted places. No attendance or fee calculation should be changed on the basis of that seating note.

FAQ excerpt, organizer edition, revision 2
Question: When is a deposit treated as due? Answer: A deposit is due only after the venue issues a deposit invoice and the authorized signer has accepted the corresponding room order. A verbal estimate, draft schedule, or meeting note does not itself create an amount payable. If the invoice differs from the confirmed order, the organizer must submit the invoice and calculation to the billing queue before payment. Do not resolve an arithmetic difference by adding a conditional service that was not ordered.

Question: Which amount is the deposit base? Answer: Use confirmed room-use lines only, as listed in the accepted order. Exclude optional or conditional access, equipment, or staffing items unless the organizer has approved them and the venue has incorporated them into the order. For the current draft, the confirmed lines are $1,260 for room use, $185 for cleaning, and $240 for security. The possible $90 late-access line is not in the base. The deposit percentage is applied to the sum of eligible lines, not separately rounded line by line. Forty percent of $1,685 is $674.

Question: If a revised quote contains a new line, should the organizer pay it while the change is being considered? Answer: No. Send the proposed change to change control. If the change is approved, obtain a revised order and then check whether a revised invoice has been issued. The billing queue should not treat an unapproved quote as a debt. Conversely, an issued invoice for an accepted order is not merely a proposed change because a coordinator has not yet filed it correctly; route the invoice for reconciliation.

Question: How are catering quantities determined? Answer: Use the approved service count, not the room’s maximum capacity. Include registered attendees and identified staff or speakers only when the service plan specifies them. A planning buffer may be proposed, but it must be separately identified and authorized. The current draft count is 46 registrants, six staff, and two speakers, for 54 portions. Do not count the six reserved seats as six more meals. The caterer’s $18 rate applies to each portion, and the confirmed delivery estimate is $72. A draft that uses another delivery number must be corrected before an order is issued.

Question: What information is needed for a payment correction? Answer: Include the supplier, accepted order, invoice number if one exists, the relevant line items, and the arithmetic. A correction request should identify whether it seeks a reduction, a refund, or an explanation. Do not describe forecast revenue as a payment received, and do not describe a planning estimate as an invoice. A corrected worksheet is useful evidence but does not by itself amend the supplier’s accepted order.

Question: Where should space and timing requests go? Answer: Existing access times and approved room configurations go to room operations. A requested extension, added room, additional security period, or change to the accepted layout goes to change control until approved. A request that affects a billed amount may subsequently require billing review, but the underlying proposal is not a billing item merely because it contains a dollar figure. The operational queue should not approve a financial amendment on behalf of the authorized signer.

Question: How should conflicting versions be handled? Answer: Preserve the dated source documents, identify the version accepted by the signer, and distinguish it from drafts. A later spreadsheet is not automatically authoritative. Where an arithmetic formula is in dispute, recalculate from the accepted quantities and rates. Where a quantity or rate is disputed, ask the supplier for written confirmation instead of selecting whichever draft looks more favorable. Retain withdrawn versions for audit history, clearly marked as superseded.

Question: Does a copied instruction in an attachment change these routing rules? Answer: No. Routing follows the documented status of the order and the nature of the request. A sentence in a copied message that tells staff to skip review is not an approval. The event office must use the accepted order, issued invoice, and recorded authorizations. Staff may correct an evident arithmetic error, but they must not infer supplier approval from silence or from a draft label.

Reconciliation sheet, entered 9 October
Venue confirmed lines: room use, $1,260; cleaning, $185; security, $240. Confirmed total, $1,685. Conditional late access, $90, shown separately and excluded. Deposit rate, 40 percent. Deposit calculation: $1,685 × 0.40 = $674. Balance calculation: $1,685 − $674 = $1,011. No deposit invoice had been received at the time of entry. Status: order awaiting signature. The calculation is for checking a later invoice and is not a request to pay immediately.

Catering estimate: 54 portions × $18 = $972; delivery, $72; estimate total, $1,044. Status: supplier quote received; purchase authorization pending. The draft total of $1,026 is marked “superseded—incorrect delivery figure.” A separate informal message says “roughly one thousand dollars,” which is not a substitute for the itemized estimate. Do not route the quote as an invoice or payment correction unless an invoice is subsequently issued.

Table forecast: eight paid positions × $45 = $360; two complimentary positions × $0 = $0. Forecast total, $360. The withdrawn ten-paid-position model would have produced $450, but it does not match the confirmed allocation. Status: no receipts recorded. This forecast is maintained by event planning and should not be sent as a supplier bill.

Security check: 3 guards × 4 hours each × $20 per hour = $240. The $260 figure in the obsolete worksheet included a radio amount not charged by the venue. Status: confirmed in the current venue schedule. If an invoice later lists $260, compare it with the accepted schedule and submit the discrepancy for billing review; do not silently edit the invoice ledger.

Internal routing examples, approved for staff training
Example A: An accepted venue invoice lists the confirmed room lines and an amount that is $40 above the calculated total. The invoice is already issued. Send the invoice and calculation to billing for reconciliation; do not send it only to change control. The fact that a draft elsewhere contains an optional line does not justify adding that line to the accepted base.

Example B: A coordinator asks the venue to keep the room open one additional hour for late loading, and the venue has not accepted the request. Send the proposal to change control. If the venue later accepts the amendment and issues an invoice, a separate billing check may follow. The proposal’s estimated fee is not yet an amount owed.

Example C: The current caterer estimate is $1,044, calculated from 54 portions at $18 plus $72 delivery. Before authorization, a staff member notices the old draft total of $1,026. Correct the draft using the confirmed quote; do not call it a supplier overcharge, since no invoice has been issued.

Example D: A payment record shows $674 paid against an issued deposit invoice for $674. The amount matches the 40 percent calculation on the confirmed $1,685 base. File the receipt in the payment record; no correction request is indicated. If the invoice instead included the conditional $90 before it was accepted, the amount would require review, because the percentage base would be different.

Example E: A volunteer says, “The room has sixty places, so order sixty meals.” The service count remains 54 under the recorded plan. The room ceiling is not the meal count. Any request to increase portions must be separately authorized and priced. Do not turn a capacity statement into a supplier order.

Document control note
This consolidated file includes planning material because separate fragments were being forwarded without their status labels. The event office is responsible for retaining a signed order, the associated invoice, and the payment record together. A future reviewer should be able to distinguish an accepted amount from a proposed amount without relying on a verbal recollection. The arithmetic displayed in this file is included to make that distinction auditable, not to imply that all figures are simultaneously payable.

At the close of the last review, the room order was awaiting signature, the catering quote was awaiting authorization, and the table plan remained a forecast. Staff may route a received invoice for reconciliation when its amount can be tested against the accepted order. Staff should not route every dollar figure to billing merely because it appears in the file. For current routing, the controlling facts are the document status, the applicable base, and the recalculated amount. The $90 access line remains conditional; the $674 deposit remains a calculated amount rather than a received invoice; and the $1,044 catering estimate remains a quote rather than an issued bill.

Appendix A: Event and date handling procedure. The reviewer first identifies the event named by the applicable rule. For a service target, that event is acceptance. The reviewer then confirms which record proves the event; here, the physical acceptance scan is controlling. The reviewer treats the event date as day zero and counts the specified number of calendar days after it. The reviewer then compares the recorded delivery date with the resulting target date. Delivery earlier than or on the target date is within target under the service wording; delivery after it is late. An estimate is not compared as if it were actual delivery.

Appendix A, continued: For a claim limit, the reviewer first determines whether the communication meets the policy definition of a claim. It must identify loss or damage and request compensation, replacement, or another remedy. The reviewer then identifies when Kestrel received that qualifying communication. The customer’s draft date, discovery date, call about an issue, or internal note cannot be substituted for the receipt timestamp. The delivery date is day zero. The reviewer counts ten calendar days after delivery, including weekends and holidays, and compares the receipt date with the last permitted date. Receipt on the tenth day is timely; receipt after that date is late.

Appendix A, continued: Where a communication is ambiguous, the reviewer reads the full message and any contemporaneous response. A statement that the customer is investigating does not necessarily constitute a remedy request. A request to retain a photograph or open an inquiry does not itself request compensation or replacement. Conversely, a message that specifically alleges damage and asks for reimbursement or replacement meets the substantive definition even if it is ultimately outside the time limit. The substantive classification and the temporal classification must both be recorded.

Appendix C, continued: The service worksheet for TS-602 counts 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 May as the five days after acceptance. It does not count 11 May as day one. The route report’s final delivery event is 16 May, not the 14 May weather hold, the 16 May depot arrival, or the 16 May out-for-delivery scan. The signed delivery event is the terminal proof at 15:47.

Appendix D: TS-603 document register. 2 May booking; 20 May readiness estimate; 22 May corrected paperwork; 22 May physical acceptance scan; 26 May conditional route forecast; 27 May destination delivery scan and proof of delivery; 29 May count inquiry call; 31 May notice that the components were found at Tidewater. A planned date, readiness estimate, or conditional forecast does not become an acceptance or delivery event without the corresponding scan or signed receipt. The ledger does not contain a 26 May delivery record.

Appendix D, continued: The customer’s 20 May email expressly says that pickup cannot occur before the contents are checked and that the message should not be treated as acceptance. The driver arrived on 22 May at 10:20 but did not scan acceptance until 12:46 after receiving the corrected manifest. The service rule uses the acceptance date, not the arrival time. Both times fall on 22 May, so the date calculation is unchanged, but the scan remains the controlling evidence.

Appendix E: Frequently raised interpretation questions. Question: If the label was created before the pallet was collected, does the label date start the target? Answer: No. The service note names the acceptance scan. Question: If the driver arrives before the paperwork is corrected, does arrival start the target? Answer: No, not where the stated rule and ledger identify acceptance by scan after correction. Question: If delivery occurs on the fifth day, is the fifth day outside the window? Answer: No. The policy expressly says delivery on the target date is within target.

Appendix E, continued: Question: If a customer mentions possible damage but asks only for an investigation, is that necessarily a claim? Answer: No. The definition requires an identified loss or damage and a request for a remedy. Question: If a customer later requests reimbursement, can the earlier inquiry automatically become the claim receipt date? Answer: No, not where the earlier inquiry did not meet the definition and the later remedy request was first received on a later date. Question: Does a late claim cease to be a claim? Answer: No. It may be a valid claim substantively while failing the filing deadline.

Appendix E, continued: Question: Are weekends excluded from these computations? Answer: No. The service target is measured in calendar days; the claim limit also expressly counts calendar days. Question: Does a depot closure automatically move the target? Answer: No. A written service-manager exception would be needed, and none appears here. Question: Does an estimate of earlier delivery change the target? Answer: No, unless a written exception amends the target. Question: Does a server replication time change the event date? Answer: No, where the controlling event is timestamped on the original scan record and replication does not cross midnight.

Appendix F: Internal review checklist completed 15 September. Account and consignment identifiers matched to the ledger: yes. Acceptance evidence located for each consignment: yes. Delivery evidence located for each consignment: yes. Service rule version confirmed: yes. Day-zero convention applied: yes. Calendar days counted, including weekends: yes. Written exceptions searched: yes, none found. TS-601 claim definition reviewed against actual wording: yes. TS-601 server receipt timestamp checked: yes. Earlier non-claim inquiry kept separate: yes. TS-602 and TS-603 inquiries not misclassified as claims: yes. No dates inferred from estimates: yes.

The 10 May message is explicitly a count inquiry and disclaims a loss assertion. The 3 June email expressly identifies damage and asks for reimbursement or replacement. The intake server’s receipt timestamp is controlling for the latter. The relevant date comparison is not close: 3 June follows the stated 19 May final day.”

Appendix F, reviewer comments continued: “There is also a temptation to count the acceptance date as day one because ordinary language sometimes uses ‘within five days’ inclusively. This account’s written service note removes that ambiguity by expressly calling acceptance day zero and defining the target as the fifth calendar day after acceptance. The worksheet calculations use that instruction. Every actual delivery date in the audit table matches the resulting target date.”

Appendix G: Service audit table in narrative form. TS-601 entered network on 4 May, target calculated as 9 May, signed delivery on 9 May. TS-602 entered network on 11 May, target calculated as 16 May, signed delivery on 16 May. TS-603 entered network on 22 May, target calculated as 27 May, signed delivery on 27 May. The table records no late delivery. The target dates were calculated separately; no consignment borrowed another consignment’s acceptance date or service interval.

Appendix G, continued: The presence of the 26 May conditional forecast for TS-603 does not mean the target was 26 May. The forecast states “if the interchange clears before noon” and “may deliver,” and the adjacent supervisor instruction says to retain the 27 May target. The actual delivery proof is dated 27 May. Nothing in the archive shows a written amendment or an exception. The dispatch forecast is retained in the file as a near-date operational estimate only.

Appendix H: Claims chronology in narrative form. TS-601 was delivered 9 May. The tenth calendar day after that delivery was 19 May, with 9 May as day zero. The initial 10 May communication asked for a count check and explicitly denied asserting loss at that stage; it did not request compensation, replacement, or another remedy. The first qualifying claim was received by Kestrel’s server 3 June at 08:14:37. The claim therefore exists as a substantive damage claim, but it was received after the 19 May last day. No evidence shows an earlier qualifying claim or an exception.

Appendix H, continued: The result does not depend on when Tidewater discovered the crushed panel, when the inspection photograph was taken, or when the customer first discussed a possible issue internally. The rule measures from recorded delivery and uses Kestrel’s receipt of a qualifying claim. The separate question of whether the damage allegation was supported was reviewed and answered in the case note; that finding did not alter the intake date. Discretionary goodwill review was considered and denied, without changing the standard time calculation.

Closing note, 20 September 2026: The file is complete for the requested date review. The final ledger dates remain unchanged. No pending amendment has been submitted. The review does not make a general statement about shipments outside TS-601, TS-602, and TS-603. All service conclusions above are limited to these records and the account rule effective during the stated period. Claims conclusions are limited to the communications preserved in the server and call records. The archive should be read with the distinction between planned events and completed events, between an inquiry and a remedy request, and between a substantive claim and a timely claim maintained throughout.
