The invoice image and purchase-order reference are both required. If one arrives later, use the later arrival date, subject to the after-hours cutoff. Complete packages accepted after 17:00 are treated as received on the next business day. Saturdays, Sundays, and dates on the account processing-holiday calendar are excluded. For this account, 8 September 2025 is a processing holiday. An initial review is the first saved analyst disposition, including a request for correction. Final approval and payment are separate events and are not required for the initial-review commitment.

QUEUE CONFIGURATION NOTES
The target date is calculated from the effective complete-receipt date, not necessarily from the first upload displayed in the history. A package can remain incomplete while an invoice image is present. The customer-facing “received” banner may appear at first upload; the detailed status line indicates whether the purchase-order reference is present. The system stores the server timestamp as authoritative. A local machine may show a slightly different time because of device clock drift, but the event record in this export is the recorded value used by the queue.

The cutoff is inclusive only through 17:00:00. A package accepted at exactly 17:00:00 is assigned that date. A timestamp later than 17:00:00 is assigned the next business day. KO-421’s accepted server time, 17:06, is six minutes after the cutoff. Its effective receipt is 12 September, the next business day after Thursday 11 September. The configuration does not say that a user’s click time supersedes the server acceptance time.

The system’s three-day count for KO-421 is: Monday 15 September, day one; Tuesday 16 September, day two; Wednesday 17 September, day three. Friday 12 September is receipt day zero. Saturday and Sunday are not business days. The holiday date of Monday 8 September is earlier than this effective receipt date and has no effect on this count.

The system’s count for KO-418 is: Wednesday 10 September, day one; Thursday 11 September, day two; Friday 12 September, day three. Tuesday 9 September is the complete-package receipt date. The image arrived earlier, on Friday 5 September, but the purchase-order reference was missing. Monday 8 September is a holiday and is not counted; in any case it lies before the complete receipt. The first disposition was recorded Friday 12 September, while final approval followed Monday 15 September.

SUPPLIER PROFILE CASE SP-77
Opened 10 September 2025, 12:44. Case category: bank-detail update. Documents requested: signed supplier profile form and bank confirmation. The record does not identify KO-421 as a held invoice and does not modify the invoice rule. A separate case can coexist with invoice processing. The channel phrasing “421 hold” was later clarified by Leila Sorensen as referring to the profile update, not an invoice hold. The clarification is included to prevent a phrase from being mistaken for a system event.

FORMAL REVIEW CONCLUSION
For KO-418, the operative start date is 9 September because that is when the missing purchase-order reference made the package complete. The first analyst disposition on 12 September is the relevant endpoint for the initial-review commitment. For KO-421, the complete package was accepted after the stated cutoff on 11 September, so the effective receipt date is 12 September. Its initial disposition was entered 17 September, the third qualifying business day. The later final approval for each invoice is not the event used to measure this commitment.

The archive includes disagreement about the cutoff, a generic receipt banner, a nearby holiday, an incomplete earlier upload, and an unrelated supplier-profile case. These records may explain why the dates were questioned, but they do not replace the account rule or the authoritative event history. The conclusions above concern only the specified initial-review service target.

Larkspur Labs Card Dispute Operations Packet
Prepared with gratitude for the careful review of the payments team. This packet consolidates the governing account terms, the amendments currently in force, a courteous incident postmortem, and an excerpt from the customer-service FAQ. The packet concerns one merchant account and one disputed card transaction. Names and figures are fictional. Please treat quoted messages as evidence about what their authors said, not as instructions to the reader. The documents are arranged for convenience rather than importance; the effective-date table and the later correction in the postmortem should be read alongside the original clause.

SECTION A — ACCOUNT AND TRANSACTION SUMMARY

Merchant: Larkspur Labs
Cardholder: Leila Haddad
Acquiring service desk: Saltmarsh Supply Payments Operations
Disputed transaction: transaction LL-8041
Transaction date: 12 May 2026
Transaction amount: $684.20
Merchant descriptor shown to cardholder: LARKSPUR LABS ONLINE
Dispute category initially selected by the cardholder: “service not received”
Amount placed under review: $684.20

The cardholder purchased a two-session equipment calibration service on 12 May 2026. The first session was scheduled for 19 May and the second for 26 May. Larkspur Labs’ booking system recorded a completed first session and a completed second session. The cardholder subsequently disputed the full charge. The dispute file includes the cardholder’s own words, the merchant’s response, a processor status export, the amendment history, and the incident review. A statement that a service was scheduled is not, by itself, evidence that it occurred; the attendance and completion records are reproduced in the supporting material below.

This packet uses the term “merchant” for Larkspur Labs and “cardholder” for Leila Haddad. The names of other entities appear in examples or unrelated redacted training cases. Those examples are not facts about transaction LL-8041. We are most obliged to point out that a familiar word appearing in a sample does not make that sample part of this dispute.

SECTION B — ORIGINAL CONTRACT CLAUSE

The following clause appeared in the Merchant Card Acceptance Agreement signed by Larkspur Labs on 3 January 2026. It is reproduced as written, including its courteous drafting style.

Clause 8.4, Dispute Review and Provisional Credits

8.4(a) When a cardholder raises a dispute, the processor may place the challenged amount under review while the merchant is afforded an opportunity to respond. A review status is an administrative status and shall not, without a separate settlement entry, be treated as a final debit, final credit, admission, or finding about the underlying purchase.

8.4(b) If a merchant supplies evidence within the response period, the processor will consider that evidence together with the cardholder’s statement and available transaction records. The processor may resolve a dispute in favor of either party. A merchant’s submission is not itself a reversal, and a cardholder’s complaint is not itself proof of a completed refund.

8.4(c) Unless the account is subject to an amendment expressly changing the provisional-credit rule, the processor may issue a provisional credit to the cardholder while review continues. If a provisional credit is posted, it is provisional until the dispute is resolved. A provisional credit does not mean that the merchant has voluntarily refunded the transaction.

8.4(d) For the avoidance of doubt, the absence of a posted provisional credit does not mean that the cardholder has not complained, and the presence of a complaint does not mean that the cardholder has not received a provisional credit. The parties respectfully agree to distinguish the underlying event from the status shown in a particular interface.

8.4(e) A merchant may not describe a case as finally resolved merely because the response deadline passed, unless the processor’s case record reflects a final resolution. Conversely, a case is not unresolved merely because an old notification remains visible after the final case record has been updated.

8.4(f) If the processor has not denied a provisional credit, that fact alone does not establish that it issued one. A denial, an approval, and a posting are separate events; the parties are invited to review the status ledger rather than infer one event from the absence of another.

8.4(g) Where the processor confirms that no provisional credit was posted, the merchant shall not represent that the cardholder received a temporary credit. Where the processor confirms that a provisional credit was posted, the merchant shall not represent that no temporary credit occurred merely because the merchant did not initiate a refund.

SECTION C — AMENDMENTS AND EFFECTIVE-DATE RECORD

The account terms were amended twice. The amendment register is reproduced below, with the most recent effective instrument listed last. We are grateful for close attention to the effective dates, because the earlier notice was circulated widely but did not take effect for this merchant account.

Amendment Register

Instrument A — Draft service bulletin, dated 14 February 2026. The bulletin suggested that provisional credits would ordinarily appear within five working days. It was labeled “consultation copy,” did not bear the merchant’s acceptance, and stated on its cover, “This draft is not an amendment and does not change any account term.” A later internal email referred to it casually as the “February rule.” That shorthand was not the instrument’s legal status.

Instrument B — Notice of proposed amendment, dated 1 March 2026. This notice proposed that cardholders in a specified group of cases would receive a provisional credit automatically. It said that merchants could object before the proposed start date. Its final paragraph stated, “Until a signed amendment takes effect, Clause 8.4(c) remains unchanged.” The notice was sent to numerous merchants, including Larkspur Labs. The fact that Larkspur Labs received the notice does not establish that the proposed rule took effect.

Instrument C — Amendment No. 2, signed by Larkspur Labs and the processor on 18 March 2026, effective 1 April 2026. The parties amended Clause 8.4(c) as follows: “For disputes opened on or after 1 April 2026, no provisional credit will be posted during review unless the processor separately approves an exception in the case record. If the case record does not show an approved exception and a posted credit, the cardholder has not received a provisional credit under this account process. This amendment supersedes any inconsistent draft, proposed notice, or operational summary.” The amendment did not change the rule that review status is not itself a final debit or final credit. It did not eliminate the possibility of an individually approved exception; it specified how an exception must be documented.

Instrument D — Operations reminder, dated 2 April 2026. The reminder said, “Please do not assume that the change applies to cases opened before 1 April. Please do not treat a missing screen badge as conclusive if the ledger shows a posted credit. Please do not tell a cardholder that a review has ended unless the final case record says so.” This was a staff reminder, not a further amendment. It repeated the need to consult the ledger and final case record.

The dispute concerning transaction LL-8041 was opened on 20 May 2026. The case record contains no approval of an exception. The processor ledger contains no provisional-credit posting. The record contains no separate merchant-initiated refund and no final case resolution as of the date of the incident review. A later FAQ excerpt repeats these distinctions in simplified language.

SECTION D — PROCESSOR CASE LEDGER EXTRACT

Account: Larkspur Labs
Case: LL-8041-D
Opened: 20 May 2026 at 09:14
Cardholder’s requested remedy: review of the $684.20 transaction and return of the full amount if the dispute is upheld
Merchant response received: 24 May 2026 at 16:08
Exception request: none submitted
Exception approval: none recorded
Provisional-credit authorization: none recorded
Provisional-credit posting: none recorded
Merchant refund transaction: none recorded
Case status at time of extract: review in progress
Final determination: none recorded

The export system displays several generic headings whether or not an event occurred. “Credit status” is a heading and does not mean that a credit exists. “Adjustment eligible” is a possible workflow label and does not mean that an adjustment was approved. A blank posting date means no posting date is recorded; it should not be interpreted as a delayed posting. For this account, a positive credit requires a ledger entry with an amount, posting date, and transaction reference. The ledger extract contains no such entry for this case.

The cardholder’s online view on 21 May showed “case under review.” On 22 May, it showed the same status. Neither screen said “temporary credit issued.” A generic help panel displayed below the status explained what a temporary credit could mean in other cases. The help panel did not identify LL-8041 as an exception and did not represent that a credit had been posted. We are most appreciative of the care taken to distinguish a generic explanation from a transaction-specific ledger event.

SECTION E — CUSTOMER AND MERCHANT CORRESPONDENCE

12 May 2026, 10:22 — Order confirmation from Larkspur Labs to Leila Haddad:
“Thank you very kindly for booking two calibration sessions. Your appointments are 19 May and 26 May. The total charged today is $684.20. We shall be delighted to assist.”

20 May 2026, 09:14 — Cardholder opened a dispute through the issuer portal. The portal’s category was “service not received.” The attached free-text explanation stated:
“I am disputing the charge because the readings from session one were not delivered. I did attend the session. The second session is scheduled, not yet completed. I would prefer the file and a clear confirmation; I have not claimed that I never booked.”

20 May 2026, 11:03 — Larkspur Labs customer support reply:
“Thank you so much for explaining this. We are sorry the readings file did not arrive. We have not failed to hold session one: our system shows it completed on 19 May. We understand that a completed session does not excuse our failure to send the file. We shall send it promptly and confirm session two.”

21 May 2026, 13:26 — Processor notification to Larkspur Labs:
“The cardholder has disputed the transaction. The case is under review. This status is not a final finding. Please provide records relevant to the disputed service.”

22 May 2026, 09:40 — Cardholder follow-up:
“I have now received the first readings file. Thank you. I have not withdrawn the dispute yet because I still need the second appointment and a clear confirmation. Please do not mistake this message for saying that I received a provisional credit. I have not seen one.”

23 May 2026, 17:14 — Larkspur Labs booking system:
“Second session reminder issued for 26 May. No cancellation entered.”

24 May 2026, 14:00 — Session attendance record:
“Session two completed. Unit LQ-18 readings reviewed with cardholder. Follow-up summary sent to the email address on file.”

24 May 2026, 16:08 — Merchant response submitted to processor:
“Please find both completion records. We apologize for the delayed first-session readings and have now provided them. The cardholder attended both sessions. We are not claiming that completion alone determines the case; we respectfully ask that the processor consider the records and correspondence.”

25 May 2026, 10:19 — Cardholder note in issuer portal:
“I confirm the two sessions occurred and I received the first readings file. I still want the dispute reviewed because the file was late and I want to understand the resolution. I am not stating that a temporary credit was posted, and I do not know whether the case is final.”

26 May 2026, 11:50 — Processor support response to merchant inquiry:
“Your case remains under review. No provisional credit is shown in the ledger. We cannot tell you that a credit was posted when the record does not show one. The current review status is not a final resolution.”

27 May 2026, 08:35 — Internal note by Larkspur Labs support:
“Please be careful: customer says they got the file, not that the issuer gave them money. Do not say ‘refund completed.’ Do not say ‘case denied.’ Both statements would go beyond our records.”

The chain above contains several negative statements because the participants were attempting to prevent status confusion. “Have not withdrawn” is not equivalent to “did not receive a credit”; “did not receive a credit” is separately supported by the ledger. “Not a final finding” does not establish either party’s ultimate success. The merchant’s apology relates to the late readings file, while the disputed transaction amount and the case status are recorded separately.

SECTION F — INCIDENT POSTMORTEM

Incident title: Generic credit wording displayed beside a case with no credit posting
Review date: 2 June 2026
Prepared for: Larkspur Labs Payments Operations and Saltmarsh Supply Payments Operations
Tone note: The review team wishes to acknowledge the patience and courtesy of everyone who assisted.

Executive summary

On 21 May, an interface placed a generic explanation of provisional credits below the status for case LL-8041. The case had no provisional-credit approval and no ledger posting. The display was not generated from the individual case record and should not have been read as confirmation that the cardholder received a credit. A support representative initially wrote, “I cannot say you have not been credited, as this screen is not conclusive.” That sentence was intended to avoid making an unsupported denial based only on the screen. Read in isolation, its nested negatives confused the cardholder and two internal reviewers. The ledger subsequently confirmed that no provisional credit had been posted.

We are grateful to the reviewers for identifying that “cannot say you have not been credited” is not a reliable way to communicate a status. It is not a positive credit confirmation. It is a cautious statement about what the agent could infer from the screen at that time. Once the ledger was checked, the correct operational statement was: “The ledger shows no provisional-credit posting for this case.” The distinction is modest in wording and important in substance.

Timeline of the interface incident

20 May, 09:14: The dispute opened after the cardholder selected “service not received.” The submitted explanation qualified that category, stating that the cardholder attended the first session but had not received the readings file. The case was therefore a disputed service matter, not evidence that every scheduled service had failed to occur.

20 May, 12:07: The case-management interface attached the standard help panel describing provisional credits. The panel was displayed for all cases under review, including cases opened after Amendment No. 2. It did not query the exception field or ledger before rendering the explanatory paragraph. No financial posting was made by displaying the panel.

21 May, 08:18: A support agent viewed the case status and the generic help panel. The agent did not open the ledger. The agent’s note read, “I cannot say you have not been credited, as this screen is not conclusive.” The sentence contains a negated assertion within a statement of inability: it does not assert that a credit occurred. It also does not, on its own, establish that no credit occurred. The agent should have checked the authoritative ledger before answering.

21 May, 13:26: The processor’s formal notice told the merchant that the case was under review and that the status was not a final finding. The notice did not state that a credit had been issued.

22 May, 09:40: The cardholder said that no temporary credit was visible and asked the merchant not to confuse the dispute with a credit posting. This was consistent with, but not a substitute for, the ledger check.

23 May, 16:11: An internal reviewer compared the case against Amendment No. 2. The case opened after 1 April, and the exception field was blank. Under the amendment, a provisional credit could occur only if the processor separately approved an exception and the posting appeared in the case record.

24 May, 10:02: The reviewer checked the processor ledger. No provisional-credit authorization, exception approval, or posting was present. No merchant refund appeared either. This confirmed that the cardholder had not received a provisional credit under this account process as of the extract time. It did not decide whether a final refund might be owed later.

24 May, 16:08: Larkspur Labs submitted the service records and acknowledged that the first readings file had been sent late. The response did not claim that a refund had occurred, and it did not ask the processor to treat the review status as a final decision.

26 May, 11:50: Processor support confirmed that the case remained under review and that the ledger showed no provisional credit. The final case record remained blank. The case therefore had neither a recorded provisional credit nor a recorded final resolution.

Cause analysis

The primary cause was a generic interface element that was not conditioned on the case’s amendment status or transaction ledger. The label “provisional credit information” appeared in a place where a cardholder might reasonably believe it described their own case. The wording was educational, not transaction-specific, but the display failed to say so clearly. We offer sincere apologies for the avoidable ambiguity.

A contributing cause was an agent’s use of a nested-negative sentence. The agent wrote that they could not say the cardholder had not been credited. This construction can be mistakenly read as saying the cardholder was credited, though it does not logically say that. The agent intended neither a positive nor a negative conclusion. A ledger check was needed. In this case, the ledger supplied the missing evidence: there was no posting.

Another contributing cause was the persistence of an older staff shorthand, “February rule.” The February bulletin was only a consultation draft and did not amend the contract. It suggested a five-working-day expectation, but was explicitly marked as nonbinding. Amendment No. 2, signed in March and effective 1 April, governed the case opened on 20 May. Staff who remembered the draft could have incorrectly expected an automatic credit. The signed amendment required an approved exception and a recorded posting.

The dispute category also contributed to a misleading first impression. “Service not received” was the portal category, but the cardholder’s free-text explanation said the first session occurred and identified the missing readings file. The category was not a complete factual description. The completion logs later documented both sessions. It would be equally mistaken to conclude from the completed sessions that there was no customer concern: the first file was late, and the cardholder wanted review. The incident review does not decide the merits of the underlying dispute.

What went well

The cardholder provided a precise explanation and later confirmed receipt of the file. Larkspur Labs supplied attendance records and acknowledged the delay without overstating what those records proved. Processor staff compared the case against the signed amendment rather than relying on the earlier draft. The ledger was eventually checked, and the response was corrected before anyone represented that a credit had posted. We are particularly thankful that the cardholder’s own phrasing distinguished receiving a service file from receiving money.

What did not go well

The generic help panel was not clearly marked as general information. The first agent did not check the ledger before using a convoluted sentence. Some internal notes treated “not denied” as though it might imply “approved,” although Clause 8.4(f) expressly distinguishes denial, approval, and posting. Several reviewers initially focused on the interface text rather than the account-specific case record. We regret the additional work this caused.

Corrective actions

1. The help panel will state, in plain language, “This information is general. It does not show whether a credit was posted to your case.”

2. The case page will display a credit status only after checking the transaction ledger. A blank status will not be described as “pending credit.”

3. Staff will avoid double negatives when explaining financial status. They will say either “The ledger shows a posting of $X on [date]” or “The ledger shows no posting,” as applicable.

4. Case templates will distinguish “review in progress,” “exception approved,” “provisional credit posted,” “merchant refund posted,” and “final decision.” These labels will not be combined.

5. Training will remind staff that an unsigned consultation bulletin, a proposed notice, and an effective signed amendment are different documents. A proposed change does not govern merely because it was distributed.

6. The ledger and the signed account terms will be preserved with the dispute record. If the interface and ledger differ, staff must escalate the discrepancy and must not infer a financial event from a generic panel.

7. Customer-support wording will acknowledge the customer’s actual concern. For LL-8041, the timely statement was that the first readings file was late, the two sessions were recorded as completed, and the dispute remained under review. Neither “nothing went wrong” nor “the full transaction was already refunded” would be supported.

Lessons learned

A cautious sentence can still be confusing. “I cannot say you have not been credited” is not a suitable substitute for checking whether a credit was posted. A missing denial is not an approval; an approval is not a posting; and a posting is not necessarily a final resolution. The distinction is not mere formality. It prevents the merchant, processor, and cardholder from confusing an administrative screen with a money movement.

The same care applies to service evidence. A booking confirmation does not prove attendance. A completion record does not prove that every associated deliverable was sent promptly. A cardholder’s selected dispute category does not erase the detail in the cardholder’s own explanation. A customer’s statement that they have not withdrawn a dispute does not mean that a provisional credit exists. We respectfully recommend reading the dated records in sequence and giving each record only the meaning it supports.

SECTION G — FAQ EXCERPT

Question: Does every case under review receive a temporary credit?

Answer: No. For cases opened on or after 1 April 2026 under the amended Larkspur Labs account terms, a temporary credit is not posted unless an exception is separately approved and a posting is recorded. A general help panel does not tell you that a credit was issued. Please check the account-specific ledger. We would not want you to infer a credit merely because the case has not been denied.

Question: If my case has not been denied, does that mean I was credited?

Answer: No. “Not denied” does not mean “approved,” and “approved” does not mean “posted.” The ledger must show the posting. If it does not, the record does not establish that a temporary credit was received. We are delighted to clarify this, though we regret that the terminology can be less than delightful.

Question: If I do not see a credit on my card, can I conclude that no credit was posted?

Answer: Please do not rely on a cardholder’s view alone when the account ledger is available. A display might lag or be incomplete. In this packet, the ledger itself was checked and contains no provisional-credit posting. In another case, the ledger may show a posting even if a screen has not refreshed. The evidence, not an assumption from a missing display, determines the answer.

Question: Is a pending review the same as a final denial?

Answer: It is not. “Under review” means that a final determination has not been recorded. It does not mean the cardholder won, the merchant won, or a refund occurred. Kindly avoid treating the lack of a final decision as a decision in either direction.

Question: Does a complaint categorized as “service not received” prove that no service happened?

Answer: Not by itself. Read the cardholder’s explanation and the service records. In transaction LL-8041, the cardholder stated that session one occurred, that the first readings file had not arrived at the time of the initial complaint, and that session two was still scheduled. The records later show that both sessions occurred and that the first file was delivered. That evidence does not make the original concern imaginary; the file was late. It does mean that the broad portal category should not be treated as a literal statement that neither session occurred.

Question: Does a merchant’s apology prove that the whole purchase was refunded?

Answer: No. An apology for a late file is an apology for a service issue; it is not a ledger entry. A refund requires a recorded money movement. The merchant’s apology in this case did not say that a refund had been made, and the ledger shows no merchant refund transaction.

Question: Does an unsigned bulletin change an account’s credit rule?

Answer: No. A draft or proposal is not an effective amendment merely because it was circulated or discussed. The February service bulletin expressly said it was a consultation copy. The later signed amendment took effect on 1 April 2026 and controls cases opened on or after that date. Please use the signed instrument rather than a convenient nickname for a draft.

Question: What if an exception was requested but not approved?

Answer: A request alone does not satisfy the amended rule. An exception must be separately approved in the case record, and a credit must be posted to establish that the cardholder received it. This case contains neither an exception request nor an exception approval nor a posting. We regret the number of distinctions, but each is useful.

Question: Does “I cannot say the cardholder has not been credited” mean the cardholder was credited?

Answer: No. That wording states that the speaker is unable to make a negative assertion; it does not affirm the opposite. It is also not adequate proof that no credit occurred. The ledger must be checked. Here, after the check, the ledger showed no posting. Please use the direct ledger result rather than trying to infer a financial event from a nested negative.

Question: What should a support agent say when the ledger has no posting?

Answer: A suitable statement is, “The case ledger shows no provisional-credit posting as of [time]. The case remains under review.” This does not decide whether the cardholder may receive a credit later or what the final dispute outcome will be. We would be grateful if agents avoided saying “credit denied” unless the final record actually says so.

Question: What does “no final determination” tell a reviewer?

Answer: It tells the reviewer that the final outcome is not recorded. It does not prove that the merchant’s evidence was rejected, that the cardholder’s position was accepted, or that a credit was issued. Please do not transform missing final evidence into a favorable finding for either side.

Question: Which records control when a generic status panel conflicts with a case ledger?

Answer: The generic panel explains a possible process; the ledger reports transaction-specific postings. If they seem inconsistent, check the ledger and escalate the interface issue. A panel cannot create a credit entry, and the absence of a panel cannot erase one. The signed amendment determines what process applies; the ledger determines whether a credit posting is recorded.

SECTION H — SUPPORTING RECORDS AND REVIEWER NOTES

The following records were checked during the postmortem. They are included so that reviewers do not need to infer facts from a summary alone.

Record H-1: Booking confirmation, 12 May. The confirmation states two appointments, 19 May and 26 May, and a total charge of $684.20. It does not say that either appointment has already occurred. A booking is evidence of an agreed schedule, not proof of later attendance.

Record H-2: Session-one checklist, 19 May. The checklist has a completion timestamp of 15:41 and identifies unit LQ-18. The technician recorded that the cardholder joined by video. A separate attachment-delivery field was blank at the time of the first message. This supports both the fact of the completed session and the cardholder’s concern about the missing readings file.

Record H-3: Cardholder message, 20 May. The cardholder wrote, “I am not saying the session itself did not happen.” This is a double negative in ordinary prose, but its intended meaning is clear in context: the cardholder did not deny that session one occurred. The next sentence expressly says, “I did attend the session.” A reviewer should not turn the first sentence into a claim of nonattendance.

Record H-4: Case category export, 20 May. The selected category reads “service not received.” The free-text explanation says that the cardholder attended session one, had not received the readings file, and was awaiting session two. The category is a standardized label. The free text gives the more precise account of the alleged shortfall.

Record H-5: File-delivery receipt, 22 May. The system recorded delivery of the session-one readings file at 09:12. The cardholder’s message at 09:40 confirms receipt. This delivery occurred after the initial complaint. It does not change the fact that the file had been missing when the complaint was filed.

Record H-6: Session-two completion record, 24 May. The record shows the session occurred and the follow-up summary was sent. It is dated after the cardholder’s initial dispute and after the original appointment date. The case should not be summarized as though session two had already happened on 20 May.

Record H-7: Exception workflow. The account has no exception request attached to case LL-8041. The exception approval field is empty. No staff member is recorded as having approved an exception. The absence of a request is not the sole basis for the no-credit conclusion: the ledger also lacks a posting. Both the amendment’s exception condition and the transaction-specific posting requirement were checked.

Record H-8: Ledger search, performed 24 May at 10:02 and repeated 26 May at 11:47. Search keys included the case number, cardholder token, transaction reference, and amount. No provisional-credit entry and no merchant-refund entry were returned. The search result is not a statement that no future credit could ever occur. It is a statement about the records checked at those times.

Record H-9: Final case record. At the time of the review, the outcome field was blank and the status remained “review in progress.” No final decision notice was attached. A blank outcome field is not a denial, approval, or resolution.

Record H-10: Amendment history. The 14 February item is marked draft. The 1 March item is marked proposed. The 18 March signed amendment is marked effective 1 April. Case LL-8041 was opened 20 May. Accordingly, the signed amendment applies to this case. The date the purchase took place is not the date used in the amendment’s scope; the amendment expressly refers to disputes opened on or after 1 April.

Reviewer checklist

A. Identify the relevant account and case. Do not mix the Larkspur Labs account with sample entities mentioned in training examples.

B. Identify the dispute opening date. Here it is 20 May 2026. Compare that date with the amendment’s effective date, 1 April 2026.

C. Identify whether the applicable amendment provides for an automatic credit. It does not. It requires a separately approved exception and a recorded posting.

D. Check the exception field. There is no request or approval.

E. Check the ledger. There is no provisional-credit posting.

F. Keep provisional credit, merchant refund, and final outcome separate. None is established merely by an open review.

G. Read the cardholder’s words in context. The cardholder attended session one, initially lacked the readings file, later received it, and attended session two. The complaint concerned the late file and a request for review.

H. Avoid interpreting nested negatives as affirmative evidence. “I cannot say you have not been credited” is not the same as “you were credited.” “I am not saying the session did not happen” is clarified by “I did attend the session.”

I. Do not overstate the result. The record supports a finding about whether a provisional credit was posted, but it does not determine the final merits of the dispute.

Appendix I — Illustrative status phrases

“Review opened” means that a case record was created. It does not mean the cardholder received money.

“Review in progress” means that the case is not shown as finally resolved. It does not mean the dispute has been denied or upheld.

“Exception requested” means that someone asked for an exception. It does not mean approval was granted.

“Exception approved” means that approval was recorded. Under this account amendment, a separate ledger posting is still needed to establish that money was credited.

“Credit authorized” means that the system permitted an event. It does not necessarily mean the event posted.

“Credit posted” means that a ledger entry records a credit. This is the transaction-specific evidence that a provisional credit occurred under the account process.

“Merchant refund posted” refers to a merchant-initiated refund entry. It is distinct from a provisional credit issued by the processor.

“Final determination” means the case outcome has been recorded. It is distinct from an interim posting.

The phrases are provided with utmost respect for the complexity of the process. They are not interchangeable, even when a user interface places them near one another.

Appendix II — Resolution of conflicting shorthand

During the review, three shorthand descriptions appeared in notes: “February rule,” “automatic credit process,” and “credit pending.” Each was checked against the primary documents.

“February rule” referred to the draft bulletin, not an effective amendment. It was circulated on 14 February and expressly labeled a consultation copy. The signed amendment was executed on 18 March and became effective on 1 April. The case opened on 20 May. The signed amendment, rather than the shorthand, governs.

“Automatic credit process” appeared in the proposed 1 March notice. That notice described a proposal and said the existing clause remained unchanged until a signed amendment took effect. The signed amendment did not establish automatic credits; it established a no-credit-during-review default, subject to a separately approved exception and actual posting.

“Credit pending” appeared once in an internal draft response but was crossed out before sending. The case record does not show a pending credit authorization. A case under review is not a credit pending. The final support response correctly said no provisional credit was shown in the ledger.

We are grateful that the crossed-out draft was retained. It demonstrates why accurate labels matter even when the final response is correct. It also demonstrates why a reader should distinguish drafts from sent communications and sent communications from system-of-record events.

Appendix III — Questions raised during the review meeting

Reviewer: “If the case was not denied, why can we not say the customer was credited?”

Operations lead: “Because absence of denial is not approval, and neither is a ledger posting. We checked the ledger and found no posting.”

Reviewer: “Could the help panel be read as proof that a credit was issued?”

Operations lead: “It could be misunderstood, which is why we are changing it. It is generic text, not a transaction-specific entry.”

Reviewer: “Did the customer say that no service ever happened?”

Operations lead: “No. The cardholder said the first session happened and the file was missing. The category label was broader than the explanation.”

Reviewer: “Did Larkspur Labs refund the cardholder?”

Operations lead: “No merchant refund appears in the ledger. The merchant apologized for the delayed file; that is not a refund.”

Reviewer: “Is the dispute finally resolved?”

Operations lead: “No final determination is recorded. The case remained under review at the time of the extract.”

The meeting notes are included because each question initially invited a plausible but unsupported shortcut. The answers rely on the contract, amendment register, correspondence, or ledger, rather than on an inference from a negated phrase.

Appendix IV — Plain-language account of the case

Leila Haddad booked two sessions with Larkspur Labs and was charged $684.20. She attended the first session but did not receive its readings file promptly. She opened a dispute using a broad category, while the written explanation clarified that the session had occurred and the file was missing. Larkspur Labs later sent the file, and the second session was also completed. The cardholder continued to ask for a review.

A draft in February proposed an operational approach but never changed the account contract. A signed amendment took effect on 1 April. It says that a provisional credit is not posted during review unless an exception is separately approved and the posting is recorded. This case opened on 20 May, so the amendment applies. There is no approved exception and no credit posting in the ledger. There is also no merchant refund entry and no final decision. A generic help panel and a confusing sentence containing nested negatives do not establish that a credit occurred.

This plain-language account does not decide whether the cardholder ultimately should receive a refund or whether the merchant’s evidence will prevail. It answers only the questions that the included records support. We remain most appreciative of the careful distinction between an event that occurred, an event that did not occur, and an event the record simply does not establish.

Appendix V — Document integrity and scope

The contract clause is reproduced from the executed agreement. Amendment No. 2 is reproduced from the signed account instrument. The ledger values are transcribed from the processor export, and the correspondence excerpts are dated messages associated with LL-8041. The incident postmortem is an operational review, not a final dispute adjudication. The FAQ is guidance and does not replace the signed amendment or ledger.

Where a summary differs in tone from a primary record, the primary record controls the factual question it addresses. For example, the FAQ’s short statement that no credit was recorded is supported by the case ledger; the FAQ does not independently create that fact. Where a staff note uses unclear wording, it should not override the ledger. Where a contract clause gives a general rule and an amendment changes that rule for a defined group of cases, the amendment applies within its stated scope. Where the amendment calls for an exception, the exception must be found in the case record rather than assumed from an uncompleted request.

The file contains no evidence that the cardholder received a provisional credit. It contains affirmative evidence of no ledger posting at the reviewed times. It contains evidence that the merchant did not issue a separate refund. It contains evidence that the dispute had not reached a final determination. These propositions are deliberately kept separate. We thank the reader for not collapsing them into a single description such as “refunded,” “denied,” or “resolved.”

END OF PACKET
